title: William Shatner says doctor dismissed key warning sign before Stage 4 cancer diagnosis
summary: William Shatner says a doctor dismissed a lump as a salivary gland before a second opinion revealed Stage 4 melanoma that spread to his brain.
story: Shatner told Fox News Digital he is still living a ‘busy’ and ‘vital’ life and doesn't plan on slowing down soon.
William Shatner is revealing the terrifying health scare that nearly went unnoticed.
The 95-year-old actor said a doctor initially dismissed a lump before a second opinion led to a shocking Stage 4 malignant melanoma diagnosis.
"So, I had a lump and the doctor, friendly doctor, said, 'Oh, it's a salivary gland. Just massage it there,'" Shatner recalled on "CBS Mornings" this week.
WILLIAM SHATNER AND DAUGHTER MELANIE REVEAL THEY BATTLED STAGE 4 CANCER AT THE SAME TIME
A second opinion saved William Shatner's life after his initial doctor dismissed a lump. (Santiago Felipe/Getty Images)
A concerned Shatner turned to a doctor friend for another opinion.
"And he put his hands here," he said, touching his face. "And he said, 'You better get this out,’ like that."
That second opinion led to a life-saving diagnosis.
Shatner said an oncologist told him, "We got to take that out now."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Shatner said a doctor friend urged him to be seen after another doctor dismissed his concerns. (Mat Hayward/Getty Images)
He continued to explain how the cancer had already grown inside his body.
"It had spread to my brain. There were little points of light in my brain and little points of light, I think, in my lung," he said. "Stage 4."
DAVE COULIER REVEALS 45-POUND WEIGHT LOSS, GRUELING SIDE EFFECTS FROM CANCER FIGHTS
Shatner underwent surgery to remove the tumor and later completed two years of immunotherapy.
While Shatner was battling his cancer, his daughter was fighting her own life-threatening diagnosis.

Melanie Shatner Gretsch discovered a lump in her breast nearly a year before her father's diagnosis. Although a mammogram months earlier had not detected anything concerning, she trusted her instincts and pushed for another check.
Shatner and his daughter, Melanie Shatner Gretsch, battled cancer at the same time. (Barry King/WireImage)
Gretsch was later diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer that had spread to the lymph nodes in her chest.
At first, she thought she was in the clear.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"Something just said, ‘You need to check again,’" she said in the joint interview with her beloved father.
But the cancer was far more aggressive than she realized.
The "Star Trek" legend has stayed busy after his health scare, with new books, a podcast and music projects on the horizon. (Michael Becker/FOX)
"And I [would have] died because it was a super aggressive kind of cancer, breast cancer, and it had already escaped the breast wall and had gone into my chest," Gretsch said.
Her treatment was intense — months of chemotherapy, 30 rounds of radiation, a double mastectomy and a year of immunotherapy.
During her health battle, Gretsch said there was one moment when she needed her father more than ever.
"I was just in one of those moments where you want your daddy, you know, like you're little. You're feeling very little, and you're feeling, ‘This is really scary.’ And I called him," she said.
By the end of 2024, both Shatner and Gretsch were declared cancer-free.
Gretsch said telling her father the news was an emotional milestone.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It was the third time in my life I had heard him cry," she revealed.
The actor, who became the oldest man to travel to space aboard a Blue Origin rocket, has continued working despite his health scare, with new books, a podcast and music projects on the way.
Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Bob Barker allegations in explosive docuseries were 'true and then some,' former game show host says
summary: Former "Double Dare" host Marc Summers recalls Bob Barker's massive ego and cheap pay after Holly Hallstrom detailed her firing from "The Price Is Right."
story: Marc Summers, the former host of Nickelodeon's ‘Double Dare,’ appeared on ‘Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia’ to reflect on his experiences with the late ‘Price is Right’ host, sharing stories about the TV icon's confidence and quirks.
Bob Barker may have been America's beloved game show host, but Marc Summers says there was another side to him behind the scenes.
The former host of Nickelodeon's hit game show "Double Dare" recently appeared on "Nostalgia Tonight with Joe Sibilia" to celebrate the show's 40th anniversary.

During the interview, Summers was asked about the recent E! docuseries "Dirty Rotten Scandals," which examines allegations that "The Price Is Right" was plagued by a hostile work environment, sexual harassment and discrimination.
OPRAH WINFREY ADMITS SHE BEGGED TALK SHOW AUDIENCE TO BURY FOOTAGE OF WHITNEY HOUSTON ONSTAGE FALL
Bob Barker, the beloved host of "The Price Is Right," died in 2023 at age 99. In March 2026, Barker was the subject of E!’s documentary series, "Dirty Rotten Scandals." (Jesse Grant/WireImage)
Summers previously worked with Barker, who died in 2023 at age 99.

"Well, I think it’s too bad that the man’s not around to defend himself," the 74-year-old told Sibilia. "However, everything on there was true and then some. I could tell you stories off the air that make your hair curl that were true."
Summers said Barker's ego didn't disappear when the cameras stopped rolling.
WATCH: MARC SUMMERS SAYS BOB BARKER'S EGO ‘WOULDN'T FIT IN THE ROOM’

"When Dorothy Jo (Barker's wife) passed away, he kind of became a different guy, and his ego wouldn't fit in the room," Summers said. "It was all about Bob. On his dressing room door and on his dress shirts, it said, 'WGMC' — 'World's Greatest MC.' Give me a break."
Bob Barker's wife, Dorothy Jo, died in 1981 at age 57. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

Summers recalled that Studio 33, where "The Price Is Right" was taped, was occasionally used by other productions. During one such shoot, longtime "The Newlywed Game" host Bob Eubanks was filming a pilot when he hid the "WGMC" sign from Barker's dressing room door as a prank.

"So, Barker comes in that Monday to do 'Price' and refuses to go on until they find the board that says 'WGMC,' and nobody could find it," Summers said. "They called up Eubanks at home and said, 'What the h--- did you do with this thing? We can't find it.' And Bob cracked up. He said, 'It's under the couch. Just lift up the couch. It is right under there.'"
Marc Summers hosted the original run of "Double Dare" for seven years. (Penske Media via Getty Images)
Looking back, Summers described himself as a 22-year-old "idea man" who got along with Barker. But the price wasn't always right when it came to working for him.
"He had a deal at CBS when they wanted to give him a raise on 'Price,' but they didn't have enough money to pay him more as a host," Summers said.

"So, they made him an executive producer and gave him an overall deal. He was producing game shows — or trying to — and needed questions written. He called me at home and said, 'Here's the show. I need 25 questions.' I said, 'Great, how much are you going to pay me?' He said, 'Marc, it's Bob. Don't worry. I'll take care of you.'
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Marc Summers attends "The Great Gatsby" Broadway opening night at Broadway Theatre on April 25, 2024, in New York City. (Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

"So, I wanted to impress him," Summers continued. "Instead of giving him 25 questions, I gave him 50. I thought, 'Oh my God, this is going to be great.' I called him and said, 'Bob, let me come by the house and drop them off.' He said, 'No, no, just put them in the mailbox, and there'll be an envelope in there for you.'
"I wrote him 50 questions when he'd only asked for 25, hoping for a check for $400 or $500. There was a check made out to Marc Summers for the grand total of 50 bucks. So, that's the way it was."
WATCH: FAMOUS GAME SHOW HOST BOB BARKER PASSES AWAY AT 99

In March, Holly Hallstrom claimed on "Dirty Rotten Scandals" that she lost her job on "The Price Is Right" after refusing to publicly stand by Barker when fellow model Dian Parkinson accused him of sexual harassment in a 1994 lawsuit. Hallstrom, one of the show's longtime "Barker's Beauties," said producers blamed her 1995 firing on weight gain caused by medication.
Barker consistently denied wrongdoing and maintained that any relationships were consensual. Fox News Digital reached out to Parkinson for comment.

From left: Holly Hallstrom, game show host Bob Barker and Janice Pennington attend a party to celebrate Pennington's book, "Husband, Lover, Spy" on Jan. 13, 1994, at Spago in West Hollywood. Hallstrom was fired in 1995. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

"When Dian filed her suit, oh boy, that was the beginning of when everything got really bad," Hallstrom told Fox News Digital. "I thought the whole situation — all the publicity, all the media attention — I thought it was horrible. I thought it was tacky. I was glad [co-creator] Mark Goodson had died [in 1992]. He would’ve been mortified to see that kind of tacky scandal on what was a family show.

"I didn't want to be involved in it at all," Hallstrom said. "Barker wanted us to go on all these talk shows and say he was the victim and that Dian was lying. I didn't participate because I thought it was tacky. I also couldn't honestly say, 'Oh yes, Dian is lying,' or 'Oh no, Dian is not lying.' I was not present for those conversations.
American model Dian Parkinson poses in a publicity photo for the CBS game show "The Price is Right" in Los Angeles, circa 1976. (CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images)

"I just avoided doing all of Bob’s PR tour," Hallstrom continued. "Finally, I was told I would be appearing on ‘The Suzanne Somers Show,’ period. And I did. Of course, all they wanted was for me to say that Dian was lying. When Suzanne asked me if I thought Dian was lying, I just babbled some answer, and that was that.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Janice Pennington, Holly Hallstrom, Dian Parkinson and Bob Barker during a taping of "The Price Is Right." (Everett)

"But then that week, I read in the tabloids, ‘Holly says, ‘Dian is lying.’ I never said that. I called the tabloid and demanded a retraction. They printed a retraction. But that was the beginning of the big rift between Bob and me. That’s when I got on his s--- list."
Parkinson dropped her lawsuit in 1995. At the time, her attorney said the legal battle had become too emotionally and financially draining and had begun affecting her physical health.

"Barker went all over television saying, ‘Her case was dismissed, and I’m totally vindicated,’" Hallstrom recalled. "I said, ‘That’s not true.’ I would not comment on that. I did not participate in those interviews. ... I would not change my testimony to suit Barker. That’s when I was told my weight was a problem. I was off the show.
Holly Hallstrom (above) was fired from "The Price Is Right" in 1995 after serving as one of "Barker's Beauties" for 18 years. (CBS via Getty Images)
"That was, well, probably the worst thing in my life at that point that had ever happened," Hallstrom admitted. "It only got worse from there."

Hallstrom and Barker spent nearly a decade locked in a legal battle after he sued her for defamation, according to Business Insider. She filed a countersuit alleging defamation, emotional distress and discrimination.

According to the outlet, Hallstrom said she was effectively blacklisted from the entertainment industry and pushed to the brink financially. She also declined settlement offers, saying she refused to be silenced by a nondisclosure agreement.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Holly Hallstrom claimed she was blacklisted after being fired from "The Price Is Right." (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Two days before Hallstrom's case was scheduled to go to trial, Barker and CBS agreed to settle, Business Insider reported. According to the outlet, CBS agreed to pay Hallstrom a settlement reportedly worth millions. The terms were not disclosed, and the settlement did not constitute an admission of wrongdoing.

"I was not going to sign a nondisclosure for that show or anything," she said. "I was not going to sign away my right to free speech. It also meant that Barker could not do to me what he did to Dian, go out and claim victory and vindication. ... He could not say anything about me as long as I could speak out for myself. And he never said another word."
TV host Bob Barker arrives at the National Arts and Entertainment Journalism Awards Gala at Millennium Biltmore Hotel Dec. 6, 2015, in Los Angeles. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images)

Not everyone accepted the show's portrayal of Barker. His longtime publicist defended the late host as "beloved" and "the greatest MC in TV history," while longtime producer Roger Dobkowitz denounced the series as an "obvious hit piece," arguing "The Price Is Right" "was a happy place" for most employees.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'American Idol' winner says husband 'put his badge up' to support her music career
summary: "American Idol" winner Hannah Harper says her husband left an eight-year law enforcement career to become her tour manager, a sacrifice she says strengthened their marriage.
story: ‘American Idol’ 2026 champion Hannah Harper tells Fox News Digital about her husband's career sacrifice, why he traded his badge for the road and how it changed their marriage.
Hannah Harper says her husband made the ultimate career sacrifice to help launch her country music dreams.

The "American Idol" Season 24 winner exclusively revealed to Fox News Digital that her husband walked away from a nearly decade-long career in law enforcement, "put his badge up" and joined her full-time on the road as her tour manager.
"It has definitely strengthened our marriage in ways that I didn't even know those muscles worked if that makes sense," Harper said.
CARRIE UNDERWOOD SURPRISES 'AMERICAN IDOL' CONTESTANT WITH TIFFANY JEWELRY AND HANDWRITTEN NOTE
"American Idol" winner Hannah Harper says her husband left law enforcement to become her tour manager as her country music career took off. (Eric McCandless/Disney)

"My husband was in law enforcement for eight years and put his badge up just so that I could pursue this," Harper said. "And he was doing insurance there for a little while. We were going to try to just do, like, a work-on-the-road kind of thing. And then music just got too busy. And he was like, 'You know what? I think I want to be tour manager.' And I was like, 'That's perfect. I think you should do that.'"

The career pivot came as Harper's schedule exploded after her "American Idol" victory, leaving the couple searching for a way to keep their family together while managing an increasingly busy tour calendar.

Harper is on her first national tour and recently landed her first major brand partnership with Sargento after her original song, "String Cheese," went viral during her "American Idol" run. The cheese company is sponsoring her tour with a custom-wrapped bus stocked with snacks for Harper, her band, crew and family.
"American Idol" champion Hannah Harper is on her first national tour and recently landed her first major brand partnership with Sargento. (Sargento/Hannah Harper)
However, working side by side with her husband has sometimes come with its own growing pains, Harper pointed out.
CARRIE UNDERWOOD WARNS HOLLYWOOD IS A 'SELF-SERVING BUSINESS,' CREDITS FAITH FOR KEEPING HER GROUNDED

"I think the biggest challenge now is because we're both working is, ‘OK, when are off hours?' You know, like when normal people go home, they're done working for the day, but our work is at home. And, so, it's hard for us to be able to turn it off. But it's so much fun for both of us to be building this together."
WATCH: ‘AMERICAN IDOL’ WINNER SAYS HUSBAND TRADED POLICE BADGE FOR MUSIC TOUR LIFE

Before being crowned the winner of "American Idol" Season 24, Harper was already building a life with her husband, Devon Mendenhall. The couple, who married in April 2018, welcomed their first son the following year and have since expanded their family to include three boys.
Hannah Harper was crowned the winner of "American Idol" Season 24. (Eric McCandless/Disney)
Harper said the family's all-in approach has become one of the most rewarding parts of her success.
"My entire family is on the road with me — both of my brothers, my parents, my kids. And I think it's so special that everyone has a role and a job, and everyone feels included."
Sargento is sponsoring Harper's tour after her original song, "String Cheese," went viral during her "American Idol" run. (Sargento/Hannah Harper)
The singer became emotional, reflecting on her husband's sacrifice.

"But more than anything, I feel honored that he was willing to step down from his position. A lot of men wouldn't do that. I think their pride would get in the way, and that man would bend over backwards for anything that I asked him to do."
WATCH: 'AMERICAN IDOL' WINNER CREDITS CARRIE UNDERWOOD FOR HELPING HER NAVIGATE FAME
As Harper adjusts to her rapid rise in country music, she said fellow "American Idol" winner Carrie Underwood offered advice that has helped her navigate the pressures of fame without losing herself.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Carrie, just saying like social media, the stage presence that one has to have, it's like a character basically, and you have to separate that character from reality, which is hard for me because I want them to be the same.
Carrie Underwood gave Hannah Harper some advice after she won "American Idol." ( Eric McCandless/Disney via Getty Images)

"I want everyone to feel connected to me and know that I'm real and authentic, but there definitely has to be a separation on my stage mask and mom if that makes sense. And, so, I'm learning that very quickly and how important it is to be able to take it off and still be mom and still be the Hannah I was before 'American Idol.'"
Harper said one of the biggest surprises since her "American Idol" win was watching "String Cheese" take on a life of its own.
WATCH: 'AMERICAN IDOL' WINNER REVEALS HOW VIRAL SONG KEEPS REOPENING HER DEEPEST WOUNDS
The deeply personal song, inspired by her experience with motherhood and postpartum depression, has become an anthem for parents who see themselves in its message.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"I am so emotionally connected to the people who are going through it," Harper said.
Hannah Harper performing on "American Idol" earlier this year. (Frank Micelotta/Disney)

"In meet-and-greet lines ... there are at least 50 of those are women who walked the exact same path as I did when it came to postpartum depression or just being in the trenches of motherhood. And getting to connect with them during their hardships. ... I relive all of those same emotions while talking to them and it still feels fresh."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Harper believes the song's impact extends beyond music.

"And I think that it's a song that continues to give, and I didn't write it on my own. I think the Lord just kind of like laid it in my lap, and He's used it to minister to people as well as me."Harper will remain on the road through November for her first national tour with upcoming stops across the country and appearances alongside Brad Paisley and Lauren Alaina.
Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Baywatch' star Brandy Ledford shares fitness secrets at 57, says she's 'not ready to hang up my bikini yet'
summary: Brandy Ledford revealed her fitness routine now centers on heavy weight training for bone density and shares the beauty secrets behind her ageless look.
story: The actress reveals why strength training has become the foundation of her health, confidence and longevity. Ledford also weighs in on the upcoming ‘Baywatch’ reboot and shares her advice for the new cast.
Brandy Ledford has no problem revealing the secrets behind her youthful glow.
The "Baywatch: Hawaii" alum said her beauty routine boils down to two Bs: "Botox and bleach."

The star, 57, who made hearts race as lifeguard Dawn Masterton, is hosting a luxury wellness retreat for women in September. She is also a creator on Passes, where she shares exclusive content and connects directly with fans.
JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'
"Baywatch: Hawaii" alum Brandy Ledford, now a content creator on Passes, previously spoke to Fox News Digital about her sobriety journey. (Caroline Malouf)
Ledford told Fox News Digital she has zero qualms about still being recognized as a sex symbol by fans today.
"I love, I mean, I'm a grandmother," she gushed. "I mean, what? That's so great! I think it's so fun. I'm not ready to hang up my bikini yet."
As she has gotten older, Ledford said her fitness philosophy has evolved.
Brandy Ledford doesn't mind being called a sex symbol. (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)

"My fitness routine these days focuses on strength training more than ever," she said. "When you get to be my age, you need to lift weights for bone density and longevity. My doctor is really stressing weight training using heavier weights for me."
WATCH: ‘BAYWATCH: HAWAII’ ALUM BRANDY LEDFORD REVEALS HER FITNESS SECRETS
"For the last few years, I was pretty addicted to yoga sculpt, a high-intensity yoga workout with light weights. I'm really trying to use much heavier weights now to strengthen my bones and muscles.
"I also still love walking, and I still love yoga," Ledford said. "I love to go on hikes. But I'd say right now I'm really, really, really focused on serious weight training."
Brandy Ledford still does yoga daily, along with weightlifting, to look and feel her best. (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)
Ledford's commitment to fitness is not new. Looking back, she said landing "Baywatch" required her to kick one unhealthy habit.
WATCH: ‘BAYWATCH’ STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS FAITH HELPED TRANSFORM HER SOBRIETY JOURNEY

"I'm a really good swimmer," she said. "I'm from the beach, so we grew up swimming in the ocean. But at the time, I was a smoker, and there were stamina tests. They would throw quarters to the bottom of the deep end of the pool, and you'd have to swim down. They wanted to see how long you could hold your breath. It was kind of hard for me at the time, so I quit smoking."
Brandy Ledford gave up smoking after she was cast in "Baywatch." (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)
"I did end up getting a lot better at holding my breath underwater and became a lot better at swimming," she added.
Ledford also "hired a trainer immediately" to make sure she always looked swimsuit-ready for every scene.
Brandy Ledford as Dawn Masterton in "Baywatch: Hawaii" (Zuma Press Inc./Alamy)

"He trained me in the water and got me really comfortable working and exercising in the water," she said. "Then I worked out with weights. I also did a lot of workouts in the sand. The sand is an incredible workout. Even walking in the sand is a great workout. And when we got to Hawaii, we worked out at the gym there.

"I just trained a lot," she said. "I really wanted to be comfortable in my swimsuit and not be self-conscious. I think that shows. When you're self-conscious, it shows. So, I wanted to feel comfortable, and the only way I knew how was to work out and take care of my body.
Brandy Ledford is a yoga teacher who splits her time between Los Angeles, Vancouver and Kauai. (Caroline Malouf)

"We all made it a priority to get our workouts in and swim in the ocean. Walking from our trailer to the set in the sand was a workout in itself. That was really important to me, and it became part of my lifestyle. I've actually maintained it to this day."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Today, Brandy Ledford is also a wellness advocate. (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)
Ledford noted she still works out daily to look and feel her best.

"I think health is our greatest wealth," Ledford said. "I really believe that what you feel on the inside is going to come out on the outside. I've been sober for 14 years, and that's been a big life changer. I have a really strong faith in God. Listen, I do all the things, but it starts from the inside. I love really good skincare. I think healthy hair is a big part of it. And I think a beautiful smile is important. I'm always drinking water."
Brandy Ledford and Carmen Electra attend the 33rd Annual Race To Erase MS Gala at Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles June 5, 2026. (Getty Images for Race to Erase MS)
The actress said maintaining her appearance involves more than workouts and beauty treatments.
Brandy Ledford told Fox News Digital she continues to lean on her personal relationship with God after getting sober. (Matt Kallish)

"I value what I look like on the outside because I value so much of the work I do on the inside," Ledford said. "I always say I do so much work in my inner life. The second I get up, I'm in prayer and meditation. I want to look as good on the outside as I feel on the inside. So, I make it a priority. But I'm just as comfortable with no makeup, sweats, a hoodie and my fluffy slippers."
Ledford said she's feeling so good these days that she's even tempted to pull out her "Baywatch" swimsuit and rock it again.
Brandy Ledford attends the 30th anniversary of "Baywatch" at the Viceroy Hotel in Santa Monica, Calif. Sept. 24, 2019. (Presley Ann/Getty Images)

"It's in storage somewhere," she said. "I might pull it out and do a photo shoot in it. It was pretty iconic — yellow — because red is what's known as the 'Baywatch' one-piece. But in 'Baywatch: Hawaii,' we wore yellow because it came from the Australian lifeguards. They wear yellow. It's not an easy color to pull off, but we had so much body makeup on that it all looked good."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Brandy Ledford and Jason Brooks in Hawaii June 1, 1999. (Zuma Press, Inc.)
Ledford said she's excited to check out the new "Baywatch" reboot, which stars Brooks Nader, Shay Mitchell and Livvy Dunne, among others.

"The advice I'd give the ladies to look glamorous and effortless on the beach in all those scenes is to stay hydrated, wear sunscreen, work out and feel comfortable in your body. They're all so beautiful, fit and in great shape. Every one of those girls looks amazing."
Brandy Ledford made her film debut opposite Sylvester Stallone in the 1993 action hit "Demolition Man." (Matt Kallish)

"I think we tend to look back at our younger selves and say, 'I wish I'd known how cute I was. I wish I'd realized I looked good in that bikini.' So, just know that you look amazing and let it shine from the inside."
Brandy Ledford attends the premiere of ABC News Studios' docuseries "After Baywatch: Moment in the Sun" at The Bungalow Aug. 26, 2024, in Santa Monica, Calif. (Variety via Getty Images)
Ledford said she isn't surprised "Baywatch" is still making a splash decades later.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Brandy Ledford attends the 6th Jam For Janie Grammy Awards Viewing Party presented by Live Nation at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles Feb. 2, 2025. (Getty Images for Janie's Fund)

"First of all, it's iconic," she said. "It's a fantasy. People got to escape. The men were hot, and the women were beautiful. But there was also drama and really good action. It was just the perfect show. I think we need that in our lives again these days."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Kelsey Grammer admits surprising reason 'Frasier' almost never happened
summary: Kelsey Grammer reveals a dinner with Paramount's president changed his post-"Cheers" plans and led to the creation of the iconic "Frasier" spinoff.
story: Kelsey Grammer reflects on starring in ‘Young Washington’ and explains why he believes the Founding Fathers' vision still offers guidance for America's future.
Kelsey Grammer is revealing the surprising twist that turned "Frasier" into one of television's most successful sitcoms.
The actor recently appeared on "Planet Tyrus," where he revealed he nearly starred in a different show after "Cheers" before one conversation changed everything.
Grammer spent nine seasons portraying the Boston psychiatrist on "Cheers," where the character evolved from Diane Chambers' love interest to one of the bar's most memorable regulars.
KELSEY GRAMMER SUSPECTS HE 'MAY HAVE' LOST HOLLYWOOD ROLES DUE TO CONSERVATIVE VIEWS
Kelsey Grammer starred as Dr. Frasier Crane on NBC's "Frasier" for 11 seasons, from 1993 to 2004. (Gale Adler/Paramount)

"It’s funny. I had visions," the star explained. "I’d been offered another show. They said, ‘We want to do a show with you when "Cheers" is over.’ They said, ‘We think you could actually carry a show on your own.’ I said, ‘Great.’ So, we actually started doing it with the same writers that ended up on 'Frasier.' We wrote a completely different story, and they wrote a script. I thought it was kind of funny.
Kelsey Grammer as Dr. Frasier Crane and Ted Danson as Sam Malone (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

"I went out for dinner with John Pike, who was the president of Paramount at the time," the 71-year-old shared. "I said, 'Have you read the script?' He said, 'Yeah. And I think a sitcom should be funny. ... This is what you guys have come up with? I don't like it. I think you should play Frasier.'
"It was John Pike who said, 'Play Frasier.’"
WATCH: KELSEY GRAMMER SHARES THE KEY TO ACHIEVING THE 'AMERICAN DREAM'
Grammer was listening.
"I said, ‘OK, I see what you’re saying. Build an audience. I am kind of funny in the character. He can’t be married anymore, and he can’t have kids,’" Grammer said.

"He did have a son. ... My thing about sitcoms is if there's a child in it, the child growing up every year becomes the most interesting thing about the show. ... Becoming a young woman or becoming a young man is the only really interesting thing that's going on in front of you. So, I got rid of that, had him come in once in a while."

Bebe Neuwirth as Dr. Lilith Sternin, Trevor Einhorn as Frederick Gaylord Crane and Kelsey Grammer as Dr. Frasier Crane appear in "The Apparent Trap," Episode 9 of "Frasier." (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

Grammer said moving Frasier from Boston to Seattle helped separate the spinoff from "Cheers." It also gave a believable reason why his young son, Frederick, wasn't part of the show full-time instead of making the psychiatrist seem like a "deadbeat dad."
"[I] just had to be a man trying to find his way," said Grammer.
"Whose support payments were on time," Tyrus joked.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Emmy winners Kelsey Grammer and David Hyde Pierce join fellow "Frasier" cast members Jane Leeves, Peri Gilpin, John Mahoney and Dan Butler for a group hug backstage at the 50th Annual Emmy Awards on Sept. 13, 1998, in Los Angeles. (Bob Riha, Jr./Getty Images)

"Frasier" premiered Sept. 16, 1993, and ran for 11 seasons before ending on May 13, 2004. The sitcom won 37 Primetime Emmy Awards and drew 25.2 million viewers for its series finale, becoming one of television's most acclaimed comedies.

In 2023, Grammer reprised his iconic role in the "Frasier" revival on Paramount+, which followed the psychiatrist's return to Boston. The series ran for two seasons before Paramount+ canceled it in 2025.
Noticeably absent from the reboot was John Mahoney, who played Grammer’s on-screen father, Martin Crane. Mahoney died in 2018 at 77.
Actor John Mahoney died on Feb. 4, 2018, at the age of 77. (Margaret C. Norton/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images)

"John was a remarkably fun guy," Grammer told Fox News Digital in 2021. "He was always kind and sweet and lovely. But the ironic thing about him — when I was directing him once on the show, I said, ‘John, let’s put the dog Eddie in your lap.’ And he says, ‘No, no.’ I said, ‘What’s going on?’ ‘He always bites me. He always growls at me. He scares me, and I don’t like it.’ So, I thought, ‘Oh, this is weird. I had no idea.’
Kelsey Grammer attends the "Frasier" SAG Screening Event Sept. 9, 2024, in West Hollywood. (Randy Shropshire/Getty Images for Paramount+)

"So, they had to put a little sardine oil on his hands, so the dog would lick something instead of trying to growl at him or bite him. This love for Eddie that existed on the show really wasn’t real. It was just an on-camera love. They fought each other, and he was really funny about his relationship with the dog.

"Every time I spoke to him, we just had a great time," Grammer continued. "We spent time in New York together off-screen, and I saw him in Chicago, and I saw him in Ireland once. He was just a wonderful guy."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Kelsey Grammer as Dr. Frasier Crane, Moose as Eddie, John Mahoney as Martin Crane and David Hyde Pierce as Dr. Niles Crane. (NBCUniversal via Getty Images)
At the time, Grammer said he was eager for what the future held, both personally and professionally.

"You know what? Life always inspired me," he said. "Life and the variety of experience is what inspires me. People inspire me; I love people. I mean, it’s odd that I ended up on a show that was based in a bar.

"My favorite places on Earth are bars. I’ve had the best experiences, met the most interesting people in bars around the world. And, so, what keeps me going personally is that there is always another experience I haven’t known.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Kelsey Grammer attends a special screening of Paramount+'s "Frasier" Season 2 at Bluma Appel Theatre in Toronto, Ontario, on Sept. 19, 2024. (Mathew Tsang/Getty Images)

"I'll go right up to the edge before it starts to get dangerous," he joked. "But I love it. I love riding horses, I love shooting guns, I love just exploring all the things that people can do and all the things that a character can do and show you. By virtue of the fact that you've played it, you've actually kind of lived it."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Marilyn Monroe role leaves actresses 'set up to fail': experts
summary: Branding experts explain why Marilyn Monroe remains Hollywood's most untouchable icon and why every actress who portrays her seems set up to fail.
story: Melissa Stevens, granddaughter of late photographer Sam Shaw, discusses the new book, "Dear Marilyn: The Unseen Letters and Photographs."
Dakota Johnson's reported turn as Marilyn Monroe is already reigniting a familiar Hollywood debate: Can anyone successfully step into the shoes of one of the world's most enduring cultural icons?
Instead of a traditional biopic, Maggie Gyllenhaal's "Flesh Impact" imagines Monroe beyond the platinum hair and red lipstick, exploring the woman behind one of pop culture's most enduring personas.

Branding experts say the reaction is part of a decades-long pattern. Every generation produces another actress willing to portray Monroe, but few escape comparisons to the Hollywood icon, whose glamour, mystique and tragic legacy have made her one of the entertainment industry's most untouchable figures. The fresh premise did little to quiet critics online, many of whom argued Hollywood should stop revisiting Monroe altogether.
"i think we have enough movies about her," a social media user wrote online as a first look of Johnson was shared.
DAKOTA JOHNSON STUNS AS MARILYN MONROE IN FIRST LOOK AFTER DIRECTOR DOUBTED CASTING

More than six decades after her death, Marilyn Monroe remains one of Hollywood's most enduring cultural icons, and experts say the actress's legacy makes her one of the industry's most difficult figures to portray. (Baron/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)
"Please leave Marilyn alone," another added. "Let her rest in peace."
"How many f---ing times y'all gonna reheat the Marilyn Monroe nachos supreme?" one user questioned.

The backlash doesn't come as a surprise to branding experts who say Monroe occupies a rare place in American pop culture that makes her one of Hollywood's most difficult figures to portray. Decades after her death, they argue, audiences still feel a personal connection to the screen legend.

"Marilyn Monroe is this irreplaceable icon that embodied glamor, mystique and tragedy. We all feel like we know Marilyn Monroe, and any actress that portrays her almost seems like an imposter," strategic communications expert Kelcey Kintner explained to Fox News Digital.
"So, it's almost as if these actresses are set up to fail, even though it's an incredibly dynamic person to play."

Dakota Johnson's reported casting as Marilyn Monroe in the upcoming film "Flesh Impact" has sparked debate online, and some fans questioned whether Hollywood should revisit the late screen legend. (Courtesy of Genesis)
One expert likened modern Monroe portrayals to an overcomplicated twist on a classic.

"Ever go to a restaurant and hear the server say ’this is the chef’s take on a cheeseburger,’ but you don’t want an interpretation, you just want a cheeseburger?" branding expert Doug Eldridge told Fox News Digital.
"It’s res ipsa loquitur. ‘The thing speaks for itself,’" he explained. "The same holds true for other iconic staples, such as Marilyn Monroe: often imitated, never duplicated."
MARILYN MONROE'S ICONIC SUBWAY GRATE PHOTO HAS SURPRISING WWII ROOTS AND HIDDEN HISTORY
Dakota Johnson will play Marilyn Monroe at age 36 in "Flesh Impact." (Matt Winkelmeyer/GA/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images)

Hollywood's continued fascination with Monroe is symptomatic of a much larger problem: an industry increasingly driven by reboots, remakes and familiar intellectual property rather than original storytelling.

"Paradoxically, Hollywood is often thought to be the home of ‘creativity’ yet much of the content being produced these days hinges on reboots and extensions of past successes," Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, said.

"How deep are we in the comic book catalog at this point. Producers are chasing that lightning in the bottle moment, but it comes with fatigue; it starts with sagging box office numbers, but, eventually, it ends when viewers become ambivalent and ratings head off a cliff.
"Creating something fresh and truly unique is an incredibly difficult endeavor, but rehashing the same narrative and storyline also comes at a price."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Marilyn Monroe's glamour, mystique and enduring cultural legacy continue to inspire new film projects, even as each portrayal draws intense scrutiny from fans and critics alike. (M. Garrett/Murray Garrett/Getty Images)
Hollywood's repeated return to Monroe is no accident. The continued fascination with Monroe reflects a broader yearning for the glamour and larger-than-life movie stars of cinema's Golden Age.

"In our age of AI and technology, it draws back to a simpler time when Hollywood icons could command so much singular attention," Kintner, senior VP at Red Banyan PR, explained. "However, I think an artist can find a new way of approaching a much-covered topic or person that brings fresh insights and makes an impact."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Despite Monroe's enduring appeal, one question continues to shadow every new project: Can anyone truly play the Hollywood legend?
"Maybe not, because at the end of the day, they aren't Marilyn and can't be, no matter their talent," Kintner mused.

"There is a longing when a celebrity has died way too young to recreate them in some way," she added. "But it always falls short because the true individual who captured the attention of the world has been lost."
One branding expert chose Sydney Sweeney as an actress that could portray Marilyn Monroe. (Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images for Lionsgate)
If anyone could do it, Eldridge picked this generation's blonde bombshell, Sydney Sweeney.

"She would be impervious to the criticism, and her gargantuan audience would translate to a box office bonanza," he explained. "It might not be critically received, but it would be a commercial juggernaut. Not only is she the logical choice, she’s arguably the only choice."

title: 'Criminal Minds' star Mandy Patinkin shares unconventional plan for after his death
summary: Mandy Patinkin revealed why his claustrophobia and Jewish heritage connected to Auschwitz make both burial and cremation unacceptable options.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Mandy Patinkin decided that when he dies, he wants his body to be composted.

The 73-year-old said on his "Don't Listen to Us" podcast that he remembered memorizing a speech from "Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, "and it was about being in a box … But the idea — I'm very claustrophobic, very claustrophobic, and the idea of being put in a box, knowing that I'm going to be in a box when whatever I'm familiar with is drastically changed is just unacceptable to me. Period. Full stop."
The "Criminal Minds" star continued, "Don't give me any business about, 'Well, you're not you, you're not here, it's a whole different thing.' Excuse me. Not OK."
NICOLE KIDMAN PLANS ON BECOMING A DEATH DOULA AS SHE ADMITS IT 'MAY SOUND A LITTLE WEIRD'
Mandy Patinkin shared his end-of-life plans on his podcast this week. (Getty Images for National Dance Institute)

And because of his Jewish heritage, he explained, "The other idea of being put in an oven is seared into my heritage genetics of the crematorium in Auschwitz, which I've visited. I can't bear the idea of being burned."

He said that while he considers himself a "conservative Chicago Jew," Orthodox Judaism dictates that "you must not do anything. You must not even let somebody do an autopsy on your body to study something, because when you go to the Olam Haba, the world beyond, you must be complete, because when the Messiah comes and everything is resurrected, and the Jews are waiting for that … you must be complete."
Patinkin joked that "you'll be in the 'Wizard of Oz' looking for the parts" otherwise.

Mandy Patinkin starred as Jason Gideon in "Criminal Minds." (CBS via Getty Images)

"I can't deal with the oven and I can't deal with the box," he said. "I love this idea so much because I don't have to be burned, and I don't have to be claustrophobic. I'm naturally put in this encasement that you've just described. I'm free to go to the Olam Haba, the world beyond, as complete. And then the organic process turns me into, you know, mulch, food, soil. And I'm not in an oven … I just am ecstatic over this."

The CEO of a human composting facility in Auburn, Washington, is seen doing a demonstration in 2019. (AFP via Getty Images)
Patinkin was presented with the idea by a woman named Robyn who came on to his podcast to discuss her husband’s wish for an earth-friendly burial.

Human composting involves putting a person’s body inside a vessel and covering it in organic material. The vessel breaks down the body through controlled heat, oxygen and moisture over a period of about a month, eventually becoming soil that is returned to the family.

title: America hits major marijuana milestone as daily weed use surpasses daily drinking
summary: Daily marijuana use among American adults jumped 21% between 2022 and 2025, with adults aged 26 and older driving the dramatic surge in cannabis use.
story: New research raises concerns about high-potency cannabis, as Fox News senior medical contributor Dr. Marc Siegel explains. Siegel highlights how increased THC levels contribute to addiction and adverse mental health effects, particularly in developing brains. He emphasizes that claims of cannabis helping with anxiety and depression are often bogus, leading to increased ER visits.
Marijuana is officially leading the pack for the most-used daily drug among Americans.

New data from the 2025 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), reveals that there are 21.4 million daily or near-daily marijuana users in the U.S.
This surpasses the 19.9 million people who smoke cigarettes and the 17.2 million who consume alcohol.
IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE

The annual federal survey of Americans age 12 and older defines daily or near-daily use as consuming marijuana on 300 or more days in the past year. Daily cigarette smokers were characterized as those who smoked on all 30 days of the past month.
The number of Americans using marijuana daily or almost daily rose about 21% between 2022 and 2025. (iStock)

The number of Americans using marijuana daily or almost daily rose about 21% between 2022 and 2025 — from 17.7 million to approximately 21.4 million. This amounts to an increase of about 3.7 million frequent users.
The biggest jump occurred between 2021 and 2022 with an increase of roughly 2.8 million users, according to SAMSHA.
This pattern in higher marijuana use is driven mostly by adults, particularly those age 26 and older, rather than teenagers.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Between 2021 and 2025, the number of adults 18 and older using marijuana daily or almost daily increased about 22%, from 17.2 million to 20.9 million.

Although marijuana is now the most commonly used substance on a daily or near-daily basis, alcohol remains the most widely used substance overall. During the previous month, about 129 million people drank alcohol while 43.8 million used marijuana.
General marijuana use rose from 13.2% to 15.1% from 2021 to 2025. (iStock)

Cigarette and broader tobacco product use has been on a decline, decreasing from 20.1% of Americans in 2021 to 15.9% in 2025. Meanwhile, general marijuana use rose from 13.2% to 15.1% during that same period.

A recent report by San Francisco-based workplace mental health platform Modern Health found a concerning increase in the number of workers turning to substances to manage stress, especially THC and marijuana products.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The survey of 1,000 full-time employees in April 2026 found that 63% of the workforce engages in at least one form of self-medication after the workday, while 52% have self-medicated during the workday.

Gen Z is the only generation of workers where THC use exceeded alcohol use after work – 59% report using marijuana products compared to 50% who drink alcohol. In that group, 51% reported using THC during the workday.
A survey of 1,000 full-time employees in April 2026 found that 63% of the workforce engages in at least one form of self-medication after the workday. (iStock)
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel said the SAMHSA data reflects a "very disturbing trend."

"Too much attention has been put on the bogus or exaggerated uses of marijuana for pain, insomnia and anxiety, when in fact it increases anxiety exponentially, especially in those with underlying mental health issues," he told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Too little attention has been paid to the growing THC content in all cannabis products, which makes it far more dangerous in terms of mental performance, judgement, memory and all forms of impairment."
THC has been associated with a growing share of fatal motor vehicle crashes, Siegel said, arguing that increased acceptance of marijuana use is "feeding a dangerous trend."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"So I firmly believe that the rising use – coupled with decreasing alcohol and cigarettes – is directly due to lack of awareness of all the dangers of marijuana versus an increased awareness of all the dangers of cigarettes and alcohol," he added.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: How often are married people having sex? What to know about the intimacy standard in America
summary: Research reveals once a week may be the sweet spot for marital satisfaction, with no added happiness boost from more frequent sexual intimacy.
story: Fox News Senior Medical Analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the alarming decline in the U.S. fertility rate to a record low of 1.56 children per couple, highlighting impacts on population size. Dr. Siegel then explains the surge in seasonal allergies nationwide due to a cold winter and wet spring, emphasizing the "hygiene hypothesis" in immune system development.
New survey data offers a snapshot of how often married Americans are having sex, while researchers say the findings challenge common assumptions about relationship health.

National demographic studies suggest that lower sexual frequency is often a normal part of aging and long-term relationships, and that there may be a "sweet spot" associated with marital satisfaction.
Data from the General Social Survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, found that married Americans report a wide range of sexual frequency.
WEIGHT-LOSS MEDICATIONS COULD IMPACT SEXUAL HEALTH IN UNEXPECTED WAYS
The survey asked how often couples have had sex during the last 12 months. Among the 1,893 married respondents surveyed in 2024, the responses were as follows.
New survey data offers a snapshot of how often married Americans are having sex, while researchers say the findings challenge common assumptions about relationship health. (iStock)

32.5% said not at all11.3% said once or twice during the year11.7% said about once a month15.3% said two or three times a month12.9% said about once a week12.2% said two or three times a week4.1% said more than three times a week
32.5% said not at all

The average American adult has sex 53 times a year — or a little more than once per week, according to research by the telehealth platform Hims.
The average American adult has sex 53 times a year — or a little more than once per week, according to research by the telehealth platform Hims. (iStock)

While marriage is often associated with less frequent sex, research has found the difference to be relatively small. A 2014 study found that married people had sex about 55 times a year, compared with 59 times a year among their unmarried peers.
"There’s no ‘perfect statistic’ or ideal amount of sex."

"Experts aren’t sure precisely why this difference exists or why what used to be an advantage has become a disadvantage, but some believe it may be related to the increasing age at which most people get married," Hims wrote in a medically reviewed article.
"There’s no ‘perfect statistic’ or ideal amount of sex. In other words: You like what you like, and that’s perfectly OK."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Clinical data suggests that aiming for a daily or high-volume sexual quota does not actually improve relationship quality.
A study published in Social Psychological and Personality Science in 2015 evaluated more than 30,000 individuals over four decades and discovered a drop-off in additional benefits.
Roughly 17% of adults aged 70 and older engage in sexual activity on a weekly basis, according to AARP data. (iStock)

While overall happiness increased as physical intimacy moved from monthly to weekly, couples who had sex two, three or four times a week experienced no additional statistical boost in marital satisfaction compared to those hitting the weekly threshold.
Experts emphasize that sexual desire naturally fluctuates as couples navigate career demands, parenthood and biological aging.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Despite some research suggesting a slowdown with age, intimacy remains an important factor in healthy aging, linked to improved physical and emotional well-being.
AARP survey data indicates that physical connection remains routine for many older Americans, with roughly 17% of adults aged 70 and older engaging in sexual activity on a weekly basis.
Reasons for declining intimacy
When a couple experiences an intimacy dry spell, medical professionals recommend evaluating physiological factors rather than jumping to conclusions about incompatibility.
Healthcare providers encourage couples dealing with mismatched sexual desire to discuss the issue openly and consult a doctor. (iStock)
Educational resources from the International Society for Sexual Medicine note that the following physical conditions can influence libido.

Rather than trying to force a weekly goal, healthcare providers encourage couples dealing with mismatched sexual desire to discuss the issue openly and consult a doctor to evaluate baseline hormone levels, medication profiles and overall metabolic health.

title: No cure, no vaccine: Experts warn of rare Bourbon virus after first NY case
summary: A Long Island patient was hospitalized after researchers confirmed the first Bourbon virus case in New York transmitted by the common lone star tick.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the alarming rise of Powassan virus, a rare tick-borne disease, with 15 cases reported this year, following a record 76 in 2025.

A rarely diagnosed tick-borne virus with no vaccine or specific treatment has been confirmed in New York for the first time, prompting researchers to warn that additional infections may be going undiagnosed.

The Bourbon virus, "transmitted through the common lone star tick, could soon begin to complicate diagnoses if it becomes more prevalent this summer and in coming years," Stony Brook Medicine warned in a news release reporting on a study of the virus.
Only six human cases have been reported since Bourbon virus was first identified in Bourbon County, Kansas, where the first known patient was diagnosed in 2014. That patient later died.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
The virus has been linked to at least two deaths, including the original 2014 case and another reported in 2026. Researchers believe, however, that additional infections have likely gone undiagnosed.
Symptoms of Bourbon virus include fever, fatigue, rash, headache, body aches and nausea. Because there is no commercially available diagnostic test, doctors have a difficult time identifying it.
Adult female lone star ticks are identifiable by a white dot, or lone star, on their backs. (iStock)
Many healthcare providers are also unfamiliar with the virus, "thus increasing the possibility of misdiagnosis," the release said.

A team of researchers led by Stony Brook Medicine confirmed the first case of Bourbon virus in New York in a patient from Long Island who developed severe symptoms and an eight-fold rise in antibody titers of the Bourbon virus. The patient was hospitalized.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There are a lot of lone star ticks in New York and in the Northeast, we have dense populations and when someone is infected with Bourbon virus symptoms they are similar to other tick-borne infections," Luis Marcos, Stony Brook Medicine professor and director of the Tick-borne Disease Clinic, said in the news release.
"For these reasons, the Bourbon virus is likely more prevalent than we think in our region, and other cases are likely not being diagnosed."
Marcos and his co-authors said their findings show the need for expanded surveillance and better testing to improve diagnosis and track the spread of Bourbon virus.
People bitten by ticks should remove them as soon as possible. (iStock)

"Without identifying the cause of an infection, the chances of developing accurate diagnostic tests or effective treatments are minimal," he said. "That is why it is so important to first understand the true impact of the virus in high-risk areas."
According to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC), "The lone star tick is widely distributed in the Northeast, South and Midwest United States."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The tiny, blood-feeding, parasitic arachnid has established populations in Arkansas, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and West Virginia, according to the CDC.
Lone star ticks are an "aggressive tick," according to the agency.
To avoid tick bites, experts advise wearing long pants and sleeves, using insect repellent and avoiding overgrown areas. (iStock)
"The adult female is distinguished by a white dot or ‘lone star’ on her back. The nymph and adult females most frequently bite humans and spread disease," the CDC reports.
Despite the Bourbon virus’ severity, "only a select few [ticks] bite and transmit bacteria, viruses and parasites (pathogens) that cause diseases in people," according to the CDC.
To avoid tick bites, people should wear protective clothing, such as pants they can tuck into boots and long-sleeve shirts.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
Experts also recommend applying insect repellent, such as permethrin, to clothing and outdoor gear, not directly on the skin.
Stay out of tall grass and on well-beaten trails whenever possible because ticks thrive in overgrown and heavily wooded areas.

Check for ticks after spending time outdoors and remove them as soon as you find them. Seek medical attention if you develop fever, rash, fatigue or other flu-like symptoms in the days or weeks following a tick bite.
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Skin condition under the eyes goes viral, and doctors warn it could signal hidden health issue
summary: Doctors reveal how low ferritin levels in the body can cause dark under-eye circles, pale skin and fatigue even as they warn against self-treating an iron deficiency.
story: Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name ‘ferritin face.’
Dark under-eye circles may be more than a cosmetic concern. Doctors say they can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media under the name "ferritin face."
Experts say there's some truth behind the trend with important caveats.

Ferritin can be thought of as the body's "iron storage vault," according to Dr. Josef Hadeed, a double board-certified plastic surgeon at Hadeed Plastic Surgery in Beverly Hills, California. It is a protein that stores iron inside the body's cells and releases it when needed.
LOW TESTOSTERONE? HEGSETH SPARKS CONVERSATION AS DOCTORS REVEAL WARNING SIGNS EVERY MAN SHOULD KNOW
"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," Hadeed told Fox News Digital.
Low iron levels can compromise skin elasticity, which can make the tissue appear thinner and less resilient, the doctor said.
Dark under-eye circles can sometimes signal low iron stores, a condition that's gone viral on social media with the name "ferritin face." (iStock)
When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable, Hadeed noted.
Symptoms of low ferritin
Besides pale skin and dark under-eye circles, other symptoms may signal that someone is lacking iron.
CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS

"The severity of these symptoms generally increases as ferritin decreases," Dane Thomas, a Texas-based hematology/oncology physician associate who specializes in the care of patients with hematologic disorders and cancer, told Fox News Digital.
Low energy, fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, headaches, fainting, brittle or thin nails, hair loss, cravings to chew ice and restless legs syndrome are a few signs, according to Thomas.

"When ferritin levels drop, the body struggles to produce hemoglobin, which is the iron-rich protein within your red blood cells that transports oxygen to the tissues," an expert told Fox News Digital. (iStock)
"Some patients also experience decreased exercise tolerance, difficulty concentrating or shortness of breath with exertion," he said.
Other symptoms can include pounding or "whooshing" in the ears, a sore or smooth tongue, rapid heartbeat, intolerance to cold and poor sleep, according to the American Society of Hematology.
Underlying conditions

Beyond cosmetic concerns, ferritin face may signal an underlying medical condition, including chronic bleeding, gastrointestinal disorders or cancers or malabsorption, according to hematological experts.

With the rise in bariatric surgery, more patients are developing iron deficiency due to impaired iron absorption, Thomas said. Certain over-the-counter acid-suppressing medications, including proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and H2-receptor blockers, may also contribute to low iron.
"This is not something that someone should self-treat."
While treating iron deficiency is important, identifying and addressing its underlying cause is equally critical, he said.

"Whenever possible, I work with my patients to determine why their iron deficiency developed so we can reduce the likelihood that it will recur," Thomas told Fox News Digital. "This often involves collaboration with gastroenterologists, gynecologists or other specialists to evaluate for sources of blood loss or malabsorption."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Pregnancy, heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent blood donation can also contribute to lower iron levels. Vegetarians, vegans and those who follow diets that do not include iron-rich foods may also be at risk, according to the American Society of Hematologists.
Diagnosis and treatment
If a person thinks they may have low ferritin, it is important to see a physician.

"This is not something that someone should self-treat, and I always advise them to seek professional help," Hadeed advised. "Unlike water-soluble vitamins, the body has no easy mechanism to excrete excess iron, and over-supplementation can lead to increased levels of iron in the body, which can affect the liver and heart."
When hemoglobin is low, the skin can lose its healthy color and appear pale, making the naturally darker tissue beneath the eyes more noticeable. (iStock)

A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. Further evaluation may include stool and urine tests to look for blood, along with endoscopy to examine the esophagus, stomach and colon. Women may also undergo a gynecological evaluation, according to experts.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Treatment for iron deficiency may include oral supplementation and, in cases of severe anemia, intravenous (IV) iron or blood transfusions.
"The biggest drawback of oral iron is gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort and stomach upset," Thomas noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"These side effects can often be minimized by taking iron every other day rather than daily, a strategy that also maintains excellent absorption for many patients."
He also recommends spacing them apart from calcium supplements, dairy products and antacids, which can affect absorption.
A simple blood test by a healthcare professional can determine iron levels. (iStock)
Following a diet that includes iron-rich foods can also help, according to the American Society of Hematology website.

Some examples include beef, pork, or lamb; organ meats like liver, chicken, turkey, duck and fish (especially shellfish, sardines and anchovies); leafy greens, such as broccoli, kale, turnip greens and collard greens; legumes, including lima beans, peas, pinto beans and black-eyed peas; and iron-enriched pastas, grains, rice and cereals.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ferritin face is reversible, Hadeed emphasized.
Once iron stores are safely restored and hemoglobin levels rebound, the skin recovers its healthy capillary flush, and dark under-eye circles tend to fade over several months.
Amy McGorry is a contributing health writer for Fox News Digital. Follow her on Twitter @amymcgorry.

title: American Red Cross declares national blood crisis as type O supply drops to dangerous levels
summary: The American Red Cross declared a blood crisis across the nation as donations hit a four-year summer low, forcing limits on type O blood distributions to hospitals.
story: The American Red Cross declares a critical national blood shortage crisis as supply levels hit dangerously low levels across the United States. Dr. Baia Lasky, medical director for the organization, joins 'Fox & Friends First' to explain the severe impact on hospitals, detail the urgent need for type O donations, and guide viewers on how to help.
The American Red Cross has declared a "blood crisis" across the nation.
The organization released a warning about the second-ever blood supply crisis this week after blood donations fell to a four-year summer low.
This decline worsens an emergency shortage that "threatens the availability of lifesaving blood for patients across the country," the organization wrote in a press release.
MICROPLASTICS DETECTED IN MOST HEART ATTACK PATIENTS' BLOOD IN STARTLING NEW STUDY

The Red Cross is now limiting distributions of type O blood to hospitals, as the nation’s largest single provider of blood products now has less than a one-day national supply of type O positive blood.
Type O blood accounts for about 60% of Red Cross blood distributions and is essential for both everyday patient care and medical emergencies.
A volunteer is pictured donating blood during an American Red Cross blood drive at Hollywood's Magic Castle in Los Angeles, California, July 28, 2026. (Getty Images)
Type O positive is the most commonly transfused blood type, according to the Red Cross, and can be safely given to about 80% of patients.
Type O negative remains the universal blood type "relied upon when every second counts."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
While thousands of Americans show up to donate blood, these donations are reportedly not keeping up with hospital demand during summer trauma season.

This summer’s conditions, amid extreme heat, poor air quality and foodborne illnesses, have contributed to lower donor turnout, the Red Cross reported. Other blood collectors have also reported critical shortages this summer.
A clinician deposits a blood collection tube during an American Red Cross blood drive at Hollywood's Magic Castle on July 28, 2026, in Los Angeles.  (Getty Images)
The Red Cross advised that just three more donors at each blood drive can end the crisis and stabilize the blood supply.
It encourages Americans to book an appointment by using the Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or by calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767).
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Biomedical Services, shared information about the developing emergency in a statement.

"The Red Cross takes its responsibility as the nation’s largest single provider of blood products incredibly seriously and has worked tirelessly to strengthen the blood supply for our hospital partners," he said.
Pedestrians walk past the American Red Cross Blood Donation Center in Boston, Massachusetts, on July 14, 2026. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)
Following the organization’s first national blood crisis in January 2022, Hrouda said the Red Cross has put "additional safeguards" in place to help "prevent a crisis like that from happening again."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"But this summer, blood donations simply are not keeping pace with hospital demand, and inventories — especially type O blood — remain under significant strain," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Every donation has the potential to help save lives, and we urgently need everyone who is eligible to make an appointment to give blood as soon as possible."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Shark Week warnings as experts reveal 6 ways to reduce your risk of a shark bite
summary: White shark activity is ramping up along both coasts this August, and experts share six critical tips to avoid a dangerous shark encounter.
story: A great white shark's powerful breach near a boogie boarder off Newport Beach early Saturday created a heart-pounding scene as onlookers watched the massive animal explode from the water nearby.
Shark sightings are common each summer from coast to coast — and though attacks are rare, they do happen.
In August, shark activity begins to ramp up as they migrate and feed along the way, often bringing different species close to shore, according to experts.

Dr. Chris Lowe, professor of marine biology and director of the Shark Lab at California State University, Long Beach (CSULB), confirmed there has been an increase in white shark activity so far this year.
SHARK SIGHTINGS SPIKE NEAR AMERICA'S BEACHES AS JULY 4 CROWDS HEAD TO SHORE FOR WEEKEND
"We expect by August, September or October to see even more sharks off the Southern California coast," he told Fox News Digital.
Even in waters where sharks are frequently found, human encounters rarely lead to bites, experts say. (iStock)

Wyatt Wernath, national spokesperson for the American Lifeguard Association and a retired ocean rescue chief based in Cocoa Beach, Florida, said they've seen typical numbers for this time of year, although there have been "a couple little nibbles" where people were "bit on the heels or the toes."
For those swimming or surfing in the ocean, the experts shared the following six tips to avoid a dangerous shark encounter.
No. 1: Know before you go
Before visiting a new beach, experts advise locating lifeguards and checking for shark sightings, rip currents, jellyfish and other hazards.
10-FOOT GREAT WHITE SHARK SPOTTED SWIMMING DANGEROUSLY CLOSE TO YOUNG PEOPLE

It's important to recognize and understand the flag systems on the beach that can signal certain conditions, Wernath noted. Red flags typically indicate high hazard, yellow flags mean heed caution and green flags mean low hazard.
Red flags typically indicate high hazard, yellow flags mean heed caution and green flags mean low hazard. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
A purple or blue flag indicates the presence of marine life. Combination red and blue flags signal hazardous marine life, such as a shark or dangerous jellyfish.
"If you can prepare yourself by knowing before you go, you’re going to have a much safer and enjoyable vacation or trip to the open water where the sharks live," Wernath said.
No. 2: Avoid other animal activity
Other suspicious animal activity in the water — such as fish, birds and even seals — could mean a shark is nearby.
"If you see the water percolating on the top, that's the fish running from the predators," Wernath said. "Don't go in the water, get out of the water."
SHARK WEEK SHOCKER AS GREAT WHITE BREACHES JUST YARDS FROM OBLIVIOUS BOOGIE BOARDER
"If you see birds diving into the water, and they're feeding kind of erratically, don't go into the water."
Lowe, who runs the California Shark Beach Safety Program, also recommends avoiding dead marine life that could attract sharks.
Other suspicious animal activity in the water — such as fish, birds and even seals — could mean a shark is nearby. (JOSEPH PREZIOSO/AFP via Getty Images)

"If you're out on your surfboard and a seal climbs on your board, that seal isn't trying to bond with you. It's probably trying to get out of the water because it knows there's a big shark around," he said.
SHARK WEEK PUTS SHARK BITE SURVIVAL IN FOCUS WITH ER DOC'S EXPERT TIPS
Avoid bait balls, which are dense schools of fish targeted by predators, Lowe advised. If one forms beneath your surfboard, move away to avoid an approaching shark.
No. 3: Don't stray too far from shore
While some "toe nibblers" in Florida have been known to attack on the shoreline, deep-water predators pose a risk as well, the experts warned.
"They might occasionally bite a person, but we don't really know why."
California has about three shark bites per year and a fatality about every third year, according to Lowe — but numbers change as the population increases and more people seek out offshore recreation.
"When people start going out into the open ocean ... they may be encountering shark species that haven't been around people before," he said. "And therefore, you're a novelty."
Fishing content creator Henry Gibbs was bitten by a grey reef shark while spearfishing in Fiji. (Getty Images)
Ocean spear fishing and kayak fishing are examples of "risky" excursions that have gained popularity in the last few decades, Lowe noted.

"Not only do you have a bloody fish on the end of your spear, but you're out around sharks that might not have been around people before," he said. "So, we just don't know how those sharks will react."
SHARK WEEK FANS MAY WANT TO THINK TWICE BEFORE EATING THIS OCEAN PREDATOR, EXPERTS WARN
"If you're kayak fishing, and you've got your legs in the water, and you’ve got a bloody fish, your leg could get mistaken by an excited shark trying to steal your fish."
When diving or snorkeling, it’s important not to present yourself "as prey," Wernath warned.
No. 4: Skip dawn and dusk swims; never swim alone
Dawn and dusk are peak feeding times for many sharks, increasing the risk of encounters.
Because sharks can mistake people for prey, Lowe recommends avoiding murky water and shiny jewelry that can mimic fish scales.
Because sharks can mistake people for prey, experts recommend avoiding murky water and shiny jewelry that can mimic fish scales. (iStock)
The chances of being bitten are statistically lower when swimming in a group than alone, Lowe said — and if trouble arises, others are there to help.
No. 5: React quickly
During a close encounter, it's important to confirm that the animal is actually a shark, as dolphin and stingray fins can look similar in the water.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Unlike dolphins and stingrays, which typically show a single fin before disappearing underwater, sharks often reveal both their dorsal and tail fins.
"Tail fins will be moving more in a sweeping motion," Wernath said. "It won't go under gradually like a submarine. It won't arc like a dolphin in a rolling fashion."
In an aerial view, a juvenile white shark swims in the clear, shallow water of the Pacific Ocean off the coast of La Jolla on Nov. 22, 2023, in San Diego, California. (Getty Images)
If a shark is identified, give it space and calmly exit the water.

"Don't splash, don't cause a commotion, which will attract the shark, but just get out," Lowe said. "If you're on a surfboard or a boogie board, try to pull yourself up onto it, and just don't present yourself as prey."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If you see the shark, always keep your eyes on it," he advised. "Follow it, track it, let the shark know you see it, turn your body toward it."
"If the shark comes closer, you can just slowly back up and keep watching it. If you lose track of it, the first place you should always look is behind you."
Unlike dolphins and stingrays, which typically show a single fin before disappearing underwater, sharks often reveal both their dorsal and tail fins. (iStock)
A shark approaching from behind is usually trying to investigate without being noticed. Once it realizes it has been spotted, however, "most of the time, the gig is up," Lowe said.
If it continues to approach, he recommends giving it "a good bop in the nose" to discourage it from coming closer.
"If the shark gets really close, I'm always an advocate of striking out at them. I think humans need to let sharks know that they're not supposed to get close to us," he added.
No. 6: Respect the species
Experts say the key to safely coexisting with sharks is respecting their habitat and behavior while avoiding actions that could make people appear to be prey.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"They're much more intelligent than we give them credit for," Wernath said, noting that they carefully assess potential prey before attacking. "They’re hunters. They're going to look around and make sure they can get to a prey without getting hurt."
The biggest misconception about sharks is that if they’re nearby, they’re going to bite you, Lowe said, adding that research proves this "simply isn't true."
CSULB Shark Lab researcher Dr. Ryan Logan spear tags a great white shark off Huntington Beach, California, on Sunday, March 9, 2025. (Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
Although human and shark populations have grown thanks to conservation efforts, shark bites haven't increased as expected.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"They might occasionally bite a person, but we don't really know why," Lowe went on. "We don't know if they're biting because they mistake us as food ... [or] because they feel we're a threat."

"Based on our last six years of data using drones, we see white sharks around people pretty much every day, and they seem to largely ignore people," he added. "What that clearly tells me is that humans are not on any shark's menu."
