Ray said he has no doubt that Kohberger committed the murders.
"If he ever does walk, he will kill again," he said.

title: Southern university requires business suits, bans du-rags and other headwear in new dress code
summary: Tuskegee University's new dress code bans du-rags, bonnets and sagging pants in classrooms as part of its broader workforce readiness push.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Retired U.S. Air Force Maj. Gen. Dr. Mark Brown, president and CEO of Tuskegee University in Alabama, is bringing forward a "professional educational environment" to one of the nation's most prestigious Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCU).

Students will be required to bring a business suit and shoes to campus for business-like meetings and cannot dress unprofessionally in the classrooms or cafeterias. Head coverings will also be barred, with exceptions for those that serve religious or medical purposes.

"The university has developed a new policy for student attire on campus, classroom attendance, and cell phone use in classrooms," Brown wrote in a message to students. "Tuskegee students now have a dress code for public and professional places."

"The Student Handbook requires students to arrive on campus with a business suit and proper shoes for a business meeting," the message said. "Students are prohibited from wearing revealing clothing in class, to the cafeteria or in official settings like Convocation. They are also not able to wear bedroom shoes, bonnets, or du-rags to class or the cafeteria."
MICHELLE OBAMA ACCUSES MEDIA OF WEAPONIZING FASHION TO 'DIMINISH' HER AS A CAMPAIGN THREAT
Retired Maj. Gen. Mark Brown was commissioned through the ROTC program at Tuskegee University in Alabama, and entered active duty in 1986. (U.S. Air Force)
The Alabama school is also restricting revealing and sexually explicit clothing as part of a broader push to prepare college students for the workforce.

"The goal here is not meant to restrict you from enjoying the Tuskegee Experience, but to prepare you with a solid foundation for the workforce you will enter once you leave Tuskegee," Brown, who took over as Tuskegee University president two years ago, wrote. "Employers are less forgiving and too often presentation may overrule stellar preparation.

"Tuskegee University continues to prepare the best and brightest for a lifetime of success," Brown added. "With these changes, we want to ensure every student is as prepared as they can be. I look forward to seeing you in August."
STUDENT LOAN RULE WOULD PENALIZE GRADUATES WHO ENTER MINISTRY, CHRISTIAN COLLEGE LEADERS SAY

Tuskegee University in Alabama is one of the most prestigious Historically Black Colleges and Universities in America and a former U.S. Air Force major general is bringing some requirements of professionalism to the campus.

Tuskegee’s fall orientation guidance lists business attire for career fairs, meetings, interviews and other professional occasions, but the guidance does restrict unprofessional attire in classrooms, too.

"Hats, bonnets, head scarves, caps, hoods, du-rags, bandanas, sunglasses, and other non-religious or non-medically required head coverings should be removed while in the classroom or cafeteria unless they are required for documented medical, religious, cultural, or University-approved purposes," the Dress Code Policy for Students that accompanied Brown's message read.

"Pants, skirts, dresses, and shorts should be worn in a manner that is appropriate for a professional educational environment. Clothing should fit properly and not expose undergarments or other private areas. Excessively short shorts, swimsuit bottoms, body suits, sleeveless undershirts, and similar casual garments are not appropriate for professional classroom settings," the guidance continued. "T-shirts worn as dresses and sagging pants are not permitted. Baggy or loose fitting pants must be worn with a belt that fits around the waist."
UNITED PASSENGER SAYS CREW ORDERED HIM TO CHANGE CONTROVERSIAL T-SHIRT BEFORE HE COULD TRAVEL
Faculty members will be authorized to respond when students are dressed in violation of the guidelines, though the president’s message did not specify potential penalties.

Some elements of the announcement reinforce standards that were already on the books. Tuskegee’s 2025-26 student handbook required students to dress "in good taste," prohibited sleepwear outside residence halls and barred men from wearing "do rags," stocking caps, bandanas, baseball caps and other headwear inside university buildings. It also prohibited sagging pants in academic facilities.

The revised rules have fueled a wider debate over professionalism, cultural expression and the expectations placed on students at HBCUs. Critics online have described restrictions on du-rags and bonnets as respectability politics that unfairly target clothing associated with Black culture.
Supporters argue that colleges should teach students how to present themselves during interviews, meetings and other professional situations.

Several alumni have defended the university’s approach. Tuskegee graduate Gwen McKinney told NBC4 Washington that the policy was "a breath of fresh air," saying there is "a time and place and a setting for every kind of dress."
White Hall is a historic building at Tuskegee University in Alabama. (Carol M. Highsmith/Buyenlarge/Getty Images)

"A critical part of being ready for and confident in business environments is being appropriately dressed," Walter P. Cooper Sr., director of the Career Education and Leadership Development Center, said.

"We know that every workplace doesn’t require business attire – our center includes business casual and casual attire, too – but as our students prepare to enter those workplace scenarios that do, it is important that access to the right wardrobe is not a barrier."
For students that might not have the proper attire, there is The Golden Tigers Community Closet to help outfit needy students.

"One of the key pillars of Tuskegee’s Renaissance Era is our focus on career readiness for our students," Brown said. "Academically, we are equipping our students to stand shoulder to shoulder with any candidates competing for roles in the global economy.
"The Golden Tigers Community Closet is an important way to ensure that every student can also feel confidently dressed when they step into those spaces."

The dress code is part of a larger set of classroom and career-readiness rules being introduced as Tuskegee expects its highest new-student enrollment in 32 years. Cellphone use will be prohibited unless authorized by an instructor.
"Faculty will be empowered to respond to students who are inappropriately dressed based on these guidelines," Brown's message to students added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Faculty will also be able to respond to a different classroom challenge – cell phones. Unless directed by the professor, students are no longer allowed to use their cell phones while in class. They should be turned off to eliminate any distraction from the instructor’s lesson."

Fox News Digital reached out to Brown's office and the university for further comment. VP of stragetic communications Thonnia Lee confirmed the details of the president's message to students and the dress code but declined further comment.

title: Florida ‘sadist’ charged after allegedly being hired by UK woman to torture and kill her
summary: A deleted video and Discord messages reveal a UK woman's final hours inside a Florida Airbnb before she was found in a shallow grave.
story: Internet searches from conman Brian Walshe and voicemails from his mother, Diana, take center stage in new Fox Nation special on the Ana Walshe murder case.
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
WARNING: GRAPHIC CONTENT

A Florida man is behind bars awaiting trial after allegedly killing a young woman who traveled from the United Kingdom to pay him to carry out their plan for her to be "sexually abused, tortured, and murdered," court records show.
Sonia Exelby of Portsmouth, England, was reported missing in October 2025 by her family when she failed to return home from a trip to the United States, records show.
Text communications to one of Exelby’s friends suggest she’d regretted her decision and wanted to back out of the deal she’d allegedly made with Hall to torture and kill her, records show.
FLORIDA MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY LURED WOMEN WITH DATING APP COULD HAVE MORE VICTIMS: AUTHORITIES

Sonia Exelby of Portsmouth, England, right, was found in a shallow grave with stab wounds in Ocala, Florida. Dwain Hall, left, has been charged in her killing. (Marion County Sheriff's Office / Facebook)
But it apparently was too late.
Days later, investigators found her body in a shallow grave in a wooded area in Ocala, Florida.
Now 54-year-old Dwain Hall of Ocala, Florida, faces charges of premeditated, first-degree murder and kidnapping. His trial is scheduled for Nov. 5 in Marion County, Florida.
Hatching a deadly plan
In 2023, Hall and Exelby met on a "fetish website" where they discussed "bondage, suicide, and her desire to have someone kill her," according to court records.
Hall, a self-described sadist, allegedly started what he described as a process of "mentoring" Exelby, investigators who reviewed their messages said.
A Facebook page attributed to Hall shows a fascination with Anubis, said to be the Egyptian god of the underworld.
In the year leading up to her death, Exelby offered to "help Hall with money he owed to the IRS," their online conversation showed, according to investigators.

They allegedly agreed that Exelby would pay him $4,000 cash to pay his debt in exchange for his help achieving "what she wanted," court records show. And they allegedly came up with a "cover story," to tell their families, and potentially law enforcement, records show.
After two years of online messaging, the young woman with a love of singing booked a flight from England to a rural area of North Florida to meet Hall, investigators said.
It wasn’t the first time she’d hatched a plan for her death, reports show.

Authorities in the United Kingdom thwarted a 2024 attempt by Exelby to travel to meet "online individuals who would be willing to kill her violently," court records show. And she had "known mental health diagnoses," investigators said.

This time, court records show, Exelby left evidence on her computer indicating that she was "again suicidal and traveling to the United States to be possibly sexually abused, tortured, and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States."
Exelby flew to Gainesville Regional Airport in Gainesville, Florida, on the evening of Oct. 10, 2025. She had a return flight scheduled for Oct. 13.
A deleted video and chilling Discord messages reveal a UK woman's final hours inside a Florida Airbnb before she was found in a shallow grave. (Sonia Exelby/Facebook)
Investigators said Hall picked up Exelby in a vehicle and took her to an Airbnb 40 minutes south in Reddick, Florida. She’d reserved it in her name, court records show.
Before picking her up at the airport, Hall purchased gun cleaner, 50 feet of rope, Lume spray deodorant, and sturdy, nylon, parachute cord at a Gainesville Walmart.
After paying for the items, he went back for one more thing—a shovel.
Those alleged details were gathered by investigators with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, who reviewed Walmart receipts and surveillance video.
‘So scared’ and ‘So broken’
On Oct. 11, after spending one night with Hall, Exelby sent "long, and at times disjointed" messages to a friend through Discord, investigators said.

Exelby allegedly wrote that "last night was so bad," and Hall had her "locked in" and had taken her phone because "he doesn't trust me with it," records show. She noted there was poor cellphone signal "in the middle of nowhere."
She fretted about regret and a gruesome choice.
"I thought he'd do it quick and not give my mind time to stew," she wrote. She said she knew it would be her last communication "if I don't take his offer of shooting him," she wrote.
In the messages, she said the person she was with "made her record three disclaimer videos and write a letter to her family because he thought it was ‘funny,’" investigation notes show.
"I'm so so scared I'm so broken and in so much pain all I can do is lay here," Exelby wrote. "I'm sorry I don't even know what I'm saying and I'm trying to be quick and my time’s up."
Missing, then found
On Oct. 11, the same day Exelby messaged her friend, Hall’s bank account for his roadside assistance business charged Exelby's debit card seven times within about 10 minutes.
After Exelby didn’t show up for her Oct. 13 flight home, she was reported missing.
Shortly after, charges to Exelby’s debit card paid to Hall’s business helped lead investigators to him.

On Oct. 17, law enforcement found Exelby’s body buried in a shallow grave in a wooded area of Marion County, court records show. Four stab wounds were found on the side of her body. The label for the shovel Hall bought at Walmart was found in the top layers of dirt, investigators said.
That same day, Hall was spotted by sheriff’s deputies and was pulled over while driving his black Jeep Cherokee on Interstate 75 in the Ocala area.
Exelby's body was found in the Ocala, Florida, area. (Photo by Nick Conzone)
DATING-APP CHARMER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER HISTORY OF DOMESTIC ARRESTS INVOLVING WOMEN HE MET ONLINE

Before being taken into custody, investigators said Hall allegedly messaged a friend over Facebook about a package he was sending that contained "precious and valuable personal items." "Will need this back in 6 months if this storm passes over with no lingering fallout," Hall allegedly wrote in the messages reviewed by investigators. "Please for the love of shadows don't lose this box."
Investigators later recovered the package contents from Hall’s friend. They found a bracelet and a black, seven-inch, steel knife "designed for piercing and stabbing," court records show.

The knife blade was engraved with the words: "Dorkworf pointy end goes in the other guy." The friend told investigators that "Dorkworf" was "making fun of Hall's use of the Darkwolf name while online."

DNA from blood samples recovered from the knife matched Exelby’s.
Initially, Hall denied to investigators that he knew Exelby, court records show.
But eventually, he described how he’d taken a video of her, but that she "was not behaving right so he deleted it."
Frightening video
Investigators later recovered the video that Hall recorded the same day Exelby messaged her friend. It had been deleted three seconds later, records show.

The 4-minute-and-16-second video shows a bruised, "disheveled" Exelby "sitting on a piece of furniture" in the Airbnb. Hall allegedly can be heard asking her questions and directing her answers, reports show. In the video, Exelby "rarely looks up towards the camera where Hall would be positioned, becomes visibly upset with tears in her eyes, exhales deeply, swallows hard, and is very hesitant to answer Hall's questions," investigators wrote in an affidavit.

When Hall asks Exelby to tell him "why she is here," she responds, "Because I'm an awful person."
When pressed by Hall, Exelby explains, "I've crushed everyone who ever loves me."

When pressed further to say how she "would want to die," Exelby hesitates, then says she wants to be stabbed.
Under his questioning, she reveals that she’s been beaten over the past days. When asked if she was coerced, she silently shakes her head.
SEND US A TIP
Hall demands, "This is how you wanted to die, right? You wanted to be beaten and made to suffer because you're such a piece of s---."
A Florida man faces a murder trial after allegedly killing a U.K. woman who went missing during a trip to meet him. Her body was found in a shallow grave in Ocala, Florida. (Sonia Exelby/Facebook)
She nods.

Hall orders: "Say it."
"I needed to be beaten and suffer cause I'm such a piece of s---," Exelby says.

"Good, good," Hall replies. He asks her if she is happy and getting what she wants.

She didn’t bring him cash and he was upset, he allegedly told them.

Instead, she gave him her debit card to charge. But he was only able to get $1,200 from it after it was declined several times. title: In-N-Out president says ‘heart is broken’ after employee, customers killed in Idaho shooting
summary: Video shows the gunman carrying a rifle toward a vehicle as the Twin Falls In-N-Out shooting left three dead and seven injured days after opening.
story: Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant left multiple people dead, several others injured. (Credit: KMVT-KSVT)
In-N-Out President Lynsi Snyder said her "heart is broken" after an employee and customers were killed when a gunman opened fire at one of the burger chain’s newest restaurants in Idaho.

Three people were killed and seven others injured, some critically, in the Saturday afternoon shooting at the In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, city spokesperson Josh Palmer said. Police found the suspected gunman dead near the restaurant, though Palmer said it was not immediately clear whether the shooter was included in the city’s reported death toll.

"We lost one of our beautiful Associates tonight," Snyder said in a statement posted to Facebook. "She was taking care of our most important asset — our Customers, and her life was taken by a disgusting human who doesn’t value the lives of others or his own."
Snyder said the gunman fired both on and away from In-N-Out property before ending his own life shortly after killing the employee and customers.
MULTIPLE PEOPLE KILLED IN SHOOTING AT IDAHO IN-N-OUT RESTAURANT, SUSPECT DEAD
This still image captured from video by a witness shows the scene of a shooting that started at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026 in Twin Falls, Idaho. (Kevin Bell Jr. via AP)
"My heart is broken, my chest is heavy, my eyes burn from the tears I’ve shed," she wrote.
TOLEDO POLICE FOLLOWING 'MULTIPLE LEADS' AS MANHUNT ENTERS 3RD DAY AFTER FESTIVAL SHOOTING
Officials had not released the names, ages or other identifying details of the victims as authorities worked to notify their relatives.
Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks provides an update on the fatal shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho. (KMVT-KSVT)
Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said investigators were also working to identify the suspected shooter and determine a motive.
"We believe the threat to the community is over," Hicks said during a news conference. "It was a very chaotic scene."
GUNFIRE SHATTERS TORONTO LATIN STREET FESTIVAL, LEAVING AT LEAST 2 DEAD AND MULTIPLE WOUNDED
The shooting unfolded at about 2 p.m. in a busy shopping plaza where hundreds of people were in the area, according to Palmer.

Video recorded from across the street appeared to show a person dressed in black carrying a long rifle toward a white vehicle. The person opened the driver’s door and then the trunk before reaching inside, prompting the driver recording the scene to leave out of concern that the shooter might be retrieving additional weapons.

Multiple victims were taken to St. Luke’s Magic Valley Medical Center. A hospital spokesperson said the facility was working with law enforcement and emergency personnel as they responded to the shooting.
This image provided by KMVT shows the scene of a shooting that started at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026 in Twin Falls, Idaho. (KMVT via AP)
The restaurant first opened on July 24, barely a week before the attack, as part of In-N-Out’s expansion into the Gem State.
Snyder said the company would mourn alongside the victims’ families and support the employees and customers who experienced the violence.
"I am no stranger to loss, but this is so incredibly tough, and my heart also goes out to all of the Associates and Customers who were there during this traumatic event," she said.
She urged the In-N-Out community to "turn to God, not in anger, but seeking comfort and strength for those who are hurting."
"We will stand together, and we will do everything we can to learn from this situation," Snyder added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are assisting local authorities with the investigation.
Twin Falls, a city of roughly 56,000 residents, is about 130 miles southeast of Boise.

title: New Mexico woman's bodycam confession about hiding newborn baby in hospital garbage tossed by state court
summary: Body camera footage shows Alexee Trevizo confessing to hiding her newborn in a hospital trash can, but New Mexico's Supreme Court ruled it inadmissible.
story: Police body camera footage captures the moment hospital staff tell 19-year-old murder suspect Alexee Trevizo and her mother that a lifeless infant was found in a tied plastic bag after the teen left the bathroom.

The New Mexico Supreme Court ruled that the body camera footage of a woman confessing to hiding her newborn baby in a hospital trash can in an attempt to conceal her pregnancy cannot be used by prosecutors in her murder case because of doctor-patient confidentiality.

Alexee Trevizo, who was 19 when she was arrested and charged with first-degree murder and tampering with evidence in 2023, was captured on police body camera admitting to hospital staff and her mother that she dumped the baby boy in the trash after workers reported the incident to authorities.

But the court ruled in a unanimous decision that all statements made in front of a police officer in the hospital room cannot be used at trial because her confession was protected under doctor-patient confidentiality, People reported. The state's high court also upheld the Fifth Judicial District Court’s ruling that surveillance video showing Trevizo inside the hospital and any body camera footage captured by police were also not admissible in court.

Trevizo’s doctor entered the room with two officers and informed the then-high school cheerleader and her mother that a dead newborn was found in the trash and had to be reported, the body camera footage shows.
NEW MEXICO WOMAN CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER DEAD NEWBORN FOUND IN TRASHCAN
Alexee Trevizo was charged with first-degree murder and tampering with evidence after her newborn son was found dead in a trash can by hospital staff. (Artesia Police Department)
"I’m sorry, it came out of me. I didn’t know what to do," Trevizo was heard saying in the footage after a doctor told her the baby was found in the trash.
"I was scared," she continued, claiming that the child "was not crying or nothing."

After learning that a newborn had been found in the trash can, Trevizo’s mother asked: "How big is the baby?" A nurse told her that the baby appeared to be full term, to which Trevizo responded that "nothing was crying."
Trevizo's mother then asked her: "Where did you put the baby at? Tell me the truth. You put it in the bag?" Trevizo confirmed that she did put the newborn in the trash bag.

Police had not read Trevizo her Miranda rights before making the confession, but prosecutors argued that she did not need to be Mirandized since she was speaking to hospital staff in front of officers and not directly to any police.
The young woman was also receiving medical treatment when officers entered the room with body cameras.

"Despite her unresolved medical crisis, Dr. [Heather] Vaskas, without authorization, ambushed Defendant, bringing with her two armed officers who stood in the doorway of her hospital room, and disclosed her personal medical information to all persons in the room without warning," the court said in an opinion written by Justice Michael E. Vigil.

Since Trevizo was "not given the opportunity to exclude anyone from the room before Dr. Vaskas discussed her condition in the presence of others" and in a "compromised medical condition," the justices said that they "cannot conclude that Defendant’s waiver of her physician-patient privilege was voluntary."

Trevizo, now 22, arrived at Artesia General Hospital for severe back pain on Jan. 27, 2023, when hospital staff began running tests and giving her morphine for the pain as they waited for her results.
The court ruled that the body camera footage cannot be used by prosecutors in the murder case because of doctor-patient confidentiality. (Artesia Police Department)

The teenager repeatedly denied to hospital staff that she was pregnant before running out of her hospital room and holding her backside on her way to the bathroom. Her mother followed her toward the bathroom and knocked several times on the locked door, waiting with hospital staff for around 20 minutes before the high school senior opened the door just as a nurse was about to unlock it.
After she opened the door, Trevizo was found cleaning up a heavy amount of blood on the floor. Hospital staff originally suspected the blood was from the woman attempting to terminate her pregnancy.
The bathroom had blood splattered on the wall, so hospital staff asked a janitor to clean it.

As the janitor was cleaning the bathroom, they noticed the trash felt heavier than expected and dug around until they discovered the newborn baby that was no longer breathing hidden inside. The janitor then told nurses of the discovery, and police were notified as required by law.

The New Mexico Office of the Medical Investigator later determined the newborn died by homicide, finding that the child died from entrapment after being placed and tied inside a plastic trash bag beneath bloody paper towels and other garbage. The autopsy report also said the child had air in his lungs and that there was evidence of a hemorrhage consistent with hypoxia.

Despite these findings, Trevizo has maintained that the baby was stillborn. She has also continued to claim that she did not realize she was pregnant until she gave birth to her child in the hospital bathroom.
NEW MEXICO TEEN ACCUSED OF KILLING NEWBORN FACES 'NONSENSE' PETITION TO BAN HER FROM COLLEGE: LAWYER
Cleaning staff found the dead newborn hidden in the bathroom trash can. (Artesia Police Department)

The district attorney’s office filed charges against Trevizo based on the conversation captured on body camera footage as well as video taken from hospital security cameras that showed her in the hospital hallway entering and later leaving the bathroom. But that evidence is now inadmissible.
After her arrest on May 10, 2023, Trevizo was released from jail and allowed to finish her senior year of high school without an ankle monitor or house arrest while waiting for trial.

Trevizo attended prom and had planned to walk at her high school graduation while awaiting trial, but the school asked her not to attend.
She then attended New Mexico State University, where students launched a petition that received more than 30,000 signatures demanding she be banned from campus.

title: Multiple people killed in shooting at Idaho In-N-Out restaurant, suspect dead
summary: A gunman opened fire at an In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, leaving multiple fatalities before the suspected shooter was found deceased nearby.
story: Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant left multiple people dead, several others injured. (Credit: KMVT-KSVT)
Multiple people were killed in a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho, on Saturday, police said.
Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said multiple law enforcement agencies responded to what he described as a "very chaotic" active shooter scene.

Hicks confirmed there were multiple fatalities, including the suspected gunman, but said authorities were still working to notify victims' next of kin before releasing an exact death toll. He added that several other people were being treated for injuries at a local hospital.
AT LEAST 1 SHOT, 1 DETAINED AFTER REPORTED ACTIVE SHOOTER AT TEXAS MALL: POLICE
This still image captured from video by a witness shows the scene of a shooting that started at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026 in Twin Falls, Idaho. (Kevin Bell Jr. via AP)

"What I can tell you at this time is that we've had a shooting at the In-N-Out location that has resulted in fatalities," Hicks said during a news conference. "I don't have the exact number confirmed. We're still trying to make notification of their next of kin."
Authorities have not released the suspected shooter's identity or determined a motive.

"We believe that the threat to the community is over," Hicks said. "The suspected shooter in this incident is deceased. He was nearby on the scene, and we are working to ascertain his identity and the motivations behind that."
Hicks said investigators are interviewing potential witnesses who were at or near the restaurant when the shooting occurred.
"We have literally hundreds of people that were in some way, shape or form in the area of this restaurant at the time that are being interviewed right now," he said.
TOLEDO POLICE FOLLOWING 'MULTIPLE LEADS' AS MANHUNT ENTERS 3RD DAY AFTER FESTIVAL SHOOTING
Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks provides an update on the fatal shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho. (KMVT-KSVT)
The FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are assisting with the investigation, Hicks said.
"Today has been a very hard day here in Twin Falls. A tragic day," Hicks said.
Police said officers responded to reports of an active shooter at about 2:30 p.m.

"Our department is responding to an active shooter incident in the area of In-N-Out," the Twin Falls Police Department said in an earlier statement. "We are asking all residents and visitors to avoid the area so officers and first responders can work safely."
TUCSON MASS SHOOTING HAS RESIDENTS CONCERNED OVER ONGOING RAMPANT VIOLENCE, POLS DEBATING GUN RIGHTS
Multiple law enforcement agencies respond to a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho. (Google Maps)
Police said the area around the In-N-Out Burger restaurant and the Twin Falls Visitor Center will remain closed Saturday evening as investigators continue processing the scene.
Idaho Gov. Brad Little urged residents to keep the community in their prayers as law enforcement responded.

"Idahoans, join me in keeping the Twin Falls community in your prayers as law enforcement and first responders respond to an active shooter situation near In-N-Out," Little wrote on X. "Please avoid the area and follow directions from law enforcement as they work to keep everyone safe."

"Twin Falls Police, Idaho State Police, and fire and paramedic crews remain on scene working to secure the area," he added. "If you're in the area, please listen to local authorities and stay away from In-N-Out and the surrounding streets so first responders can do their jobs."

title: Lettuce farmers plow crops back into soil as cyclosporiasis fears tank demand for fresh greens
summary: A California farmer was forced to destroy 300,000 pounds of romaine hearts as the cyclosporiasis outbreak crushes lettuce demand across America's Salad Bowl.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Jonathan Serrie details the multi-state cyclospora parasite outbreak traced to iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico by Taylor Farms. The CDC reports over 1,600 cases across five Midwestern states, with Taylor Farms recalling product in 27 states and halting imports from the region for the remainder of the growing season.
The nationwide cyclosporiasis outbreak has forced some American farmers to throw out their entire lettuce crops, according to a report.
One such farmer in California’s Salinas Valley told the Wall Steet Journal this week that he had to chop up 300,000 pounds of romaine hearts and plow it back into the soil.
This came with no evidence that his crops were infected with the parasite causing explosive diarrhea that has sickened thousands of people in nearly every state.
WHITE HOUSE ADDRESSES GROWING PARASITE OUTBREAK AFTER MORE THAN 400 AMERICANS SICKENED
A crop of lettuce is watered in Bakersfield, California in 2021. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Cox’s Coastline Family Farms supplies major grocery stores and top restaurants around the country, but the outbreak has lowered the demand for his greens by as much as 30%, he said.
"It is incredibly demoralizing," Cox told the Journal. "I would’ve been better off taking a vacation in the South of France than planting the crop."
The region is known as "America’s Salad Bowl" and supplies the country with nearly half of its lettuce.
CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK: IS IT STILL SAFE TO EAT AT RESTAURANTS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW
Still, he’s optimistic about the next harvest.
"You can’t afford to be downcast very long. You better pick yourself up, dust yourself off and keep pushing forward," he explained.

Although the outbreak has been linked to iceberg lettuce from central Mexico recalled by California-based Taylor Farms — the country’s largest lettuce supplier --- it’s affected the entire lettuce industry as Americans worry.
An undated microscope photo shows Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts in a fresh stool sample prepared with a formalin solution and stained with safranin. (CDC via AP)
CRUISE SHIP HIT WITH THIRD STOMACH ILLNESS OUTBREAK IN TWO MONTHS, REVIEW UNDERWAY

"Consumers aren’t sure what’s right anymore so, out of an abundance of caution, they’re just passing on everything," Joelle Mosso, a food scientist at family farm trade group Western Growers, told the Journal.
Viraj Puri, who founded Gotham Greens in Brooklyn told the Journal that, despite lagging sales, his company opted against less seeding.

"The public health benefits of a diet grounded in fruits and vegetables are indisputable," he said. "I really hope consumers can get back to trusting the fruits and vegetables they buy in stores, because they generally are safe."
Nationally, sales of fresh lettuce fell by nearly 9% in the month between mid-June and July as compared to the same time last year, the outlet reported, citing data from NielsenIQ.
That’s equivalent to 7.6 million pounds of lettuce.
Packaged salad mixes are displayed in the refrigerated produce section of a Target store in Washington, D.C., on July 22, 2026. (Getty Images)
Sales were also down on other vegetables like cauliflower, carrots, spinach and Brussels sprouts.
Even salad dressing has taken a hit.

After one outbreak of cyclosporiasis was linked to lettuce served at Taco Bell, its sales went down by 25% that week.
While some are heading to local farmers markets, hoping their lettuce is more safe, most people appear to be taking a vegetable pause.

title: Hundreds block Florida interstate in alleged street takeover before 140 mph police chase
summary: Traffic cameras captured hundreds of vehicles blocking I-75 in Hillsborough County during an illegal street takeover before a BMW fled at 140 mph.
story: Fox News correspondent Madison Scarpino reports on a violent teen takeover in Tampa, Florida, where 22 individuals were arrested, including a 12-year-old, on 'America Reports.'

Four people were arrested after authorities said hundreds of vehicles blocked all northbound lanes of Interstate 75 during an apparent street takeover in Hillsborough County, Florida early Saturday, prompting a high-speed chase that reached 140 mph.

The incident began around 1:30 a.m. near mile marker 266 in Thonotosassa, where Florida Highway Patrol traffic cameras captured a large gathering of vehicles stopping traffic while some drivers performed burnouts in the middle of the interstate, according to an arrest report.

As troopers responded to the scene, video showed vehicles rapidly dispersing as drivers and spectators rushed back to their cars, the report said. While most of those involved were allowed to leave without facing charges, one green BMW allegedly sped away from the scene, leading a trooper to initiate a pursuit.
FLORIDA MAN IN BUNNY HELMET ALLEGEDLY LED POLICE ON 120 MPH CHASE BEFORE SURRENDERING TO TROOPERS

Yulian Lugo was charged with aggravated fleeing to elude and participating in a street takeover after authorities said he fled Florida Highway Patrol troopers at speeds reaching 140 mph. (Hillsborough Sheriff's Office)
According to FHP, the BMW accelerated to approximately 140 mph — about twice the posted speed limit — before exiting the interstate and eventually stopping in a parking lot.
The driver, identified as 25-year-old Yulian Lugo, was arrested and charged with aggravated fleeing to elude and participating in a street takeover, both felony offenses, authorities said.
Three passengers — a 24-year-old and two 18-year-olds — were also taken into custody and each charged with misdemeanor highway racing, according to FHP.
All four were booked into the Hillsborough County Jail.
VIRAL TEEN TAKEOVERS UNLEASH CHAOS NATIONWIDE AS MALLS, BEACHES AND RESTAURANTS BECOME BATTLEGROUNDS

A Florida Highway Patrol cruiser is parked on the roadside. Authorities arrested four people after an alleged street takeover shut down Interstate 75 early Saturday. (Sam Navarro/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service)

Street takeovers, in which participants use public roads to perform stunts such as burnouts and other reckless driving maneuvers while crowds gather to watch, have become an enforcement focus for law enforcement agencies in Florida and across the country because of the safety risks they pose to motorists, participants and spectators.

title: Father of 10-year-old boy breaks silence after viral beach rescue: 'No way I could ever repay him'
summary: Viral video shows 16-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams diving beneath heavy surf to rescue an unconscious 10-year-old boy at Seabright State Beach.
story: Ryder Williams, a 16-year-old lifeguard, is hailed as a hero after rescuing a child caught in dangerous rip tides and powerful surf in Santa Cruz, California. The boy's grateful father speaks out, expressing immense thanks for Ryder's bravery. Williams is now invited to the White House to receive a civilian honor for his courageous actions.
Sumit Rai said he received a phone call no parent wants to receive after his 10-year-old son was swept into the ocean at California's Seabright State Beach.
"My son [called and] told me, 'Dad, I drowned. I went unconscious.' I'm listening to him, and he thinks he is going to die," Rai shared on Fox News Live.
Nathaniel was standing on the wet sand near the shoreline when a wave knocked him down and pulled him roughly 15 yards into deep water.
Witnesses say the dramatic rescue lasted far longer than the viral video shows, with Ryder Williams refusing to release the child despite punishing surf. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)
TRUMP SAYS HEROIC TEEN LIFEGUARD WHO SAVED BOY FROM TOWERING WAVES DESERVES WHITE HOUSE HONOR
Seabright State Beach was under a high surf advisory at the time. According to California State Parks, swell conditions generated 4- to 6-foot waves, with sets occasionally reaching 10 feet.

Ryder Williams, a 16-year-old lifeguard stationed at Tower 2, spotted Nathaniel losing his footing. In a statement to California State Parks, Williams said he saw the child about 20 yards from the tower.

The 16-year-old radioed in the situation, left his devices and sunglasses at the base of the tower, and ran toward the shore with fins strapped to his wrists and a buoy. He then dove into the water and swam to reach the boy.
Viral video of the rescue showed Williams holding Nathaniel in the rough surf.
CALIFORNIA LIFEGUARD SPEAKS OUT ON HEARTSTOPPING OCEAN RESCUE: 'I LOVE WHAT I DO'
"After the first wave, I was unable to pull him out because he was limp and the waves were pushing so hard," Williams said.
About three more waves broke over the two before fellow lifeguard Aaron Bohnen entered the water to assist.
Rai noted that carrying the limp child required Williams to move roughly 100 pounds through the crashing waves.
"Doing that is remarkable," Rai said. "There is no way I could ever repay him."
OFF-DUTY ICE OFFICER RELIES ON 'SIXTH SENSE' TO SAVE DROWNING CHILD BEFORE DELIVERING MESSAGE TO CRITICS
Williams and Bohnen brought Nathaniel to shore and evaluated him for injuries. Rai, who was not on vacation with his children, said he had not yet seen his son following the rescue.

"The first thing I’ll do is give him a big hug," he said. "... I’m so relieved and grateful for Ryder and his courage and heroism and going into that tumultuous condition to save my son. Without him, my son wouldn’t be alive."

Witnesses say the dramatic rescue lasted far longer than the viral video shows, with the teen lifeguard refusing to release the child despite punishing surf. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)
After the video of the rescue garnered national attention, President Donald Trump said Williams deserved a trip to the White House and a national honor.
Asked about the remarks by Fox News Live host Aishah Hasnie, Rai supported recognition for the young lifeguard.
"He absolutely should. I’m for any award or recognition," he said. "I’m his biggest fan, and I am so grateful for what he did. My children are precious to me and nothing means more to me."
FILE - U.S. President Donald Trump said he thought the teen lifeguard deserved a trip to the White House following the heroic save. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Reflecting on the value of local lifeguards in the community, Williams said he feels fortunate.

"I’m grateful to have had the opportunity to return the child to his family safely," Williams said. "This is my job and I love what I do. I’m thankful to my fellow lifeguards who perform rescues just like this every day."
California State Parks’ Santa Cruz District lifeguards performed 34 rescues over the weekend and made more than 5,000 preventative contacts along the coastline.
Sophia Leone is a guest greeter for Fox News Channel.

The facility's registered nurse (RN) told investigators Brambrink was "dead to the world" after drinking while fishing, according to an investigative report from the Department of Health.

"The night before the scheduled appointment, the resident was given 2 shots of alcohol at 6:54 p.m., 2 shots at 8 p.m., and 2 shots at 9:20 p.m. The morning of the appointment, staff gave the resident 2 shots at 3:55 a.m., a beer at 5 a.m., 2 shots at 5:55 a.m., 2 shots at 8:15 a.m., 2 shots at 9:15 a.m., and 2 shots at 10:55 a.m., and 2 shots at 12:30 p.m.," the report said.

"When someone from the PCP’s office called back to request vital signs be taken, the RN reported the resident was found down on the floor and that he 'didn’t feel right.' He was transported to the emergency room shortly after," the report claimed.
Hospital staff wanted to keep Brambrink overnight to evaluate him for alcohol withdrawal, but he refused, telling them he "would rather go home and continue to drink," the report states.
Brambrink's blood alcohol level was at 0.23%, almost three times the legal limit of 0.08%, according to the report.

The assisted care resident had numerous mental health diagnoses, including psychoactive substance abuse and anxiety, according to the report.

"The resident’s assessment indicated the resident had heard voices for 40 years and was homeless prior to moving into the facility. The resident was noted to have a history of alcohol use, drank alcohol daily, and had a history of meth use," the report said.
The facility had a written "alcohol plan" for Brambrink that stipulated he gets two shots per hour because he was "trying to drown out the voices," the report stated.

Covered Bridge's owner, Trista Barstow, defended her business's actions in an interview with FOX 9, arguing the center is one of the few that will take in what she called "extreme alcoholics."

"Under the Minnesota Resident Bill of Rights, competent adult residents have the right to make lawful personal choices, including whether to consume alcohol. That includes the right to make decisions we may not agree with or recommend, including excessive drinking," Barstow added.

"Our responsibility is not to make those decisions for residents but to educate them about the risks, assess their health and safety, monitor for concerns and respond appropriately when intervention is needed.

title: Father of slain Marine speaks out after illegal immigrant who killed son faces third deportation
summary: Martin Martinez-Ballinas, arrested five times before the fatal motorcycle crash, now faces a third deportation after illegally reentering the U.S.
story: James Walden Jr. shares the story of losing his son, LCpl. James Ray Walden III, in a crash caused by an illegal immigrant who had repeatedly reentered the U.S. after being deported, on 'The Will Cain Show.'

The father of a U.S. Marine killed in a hit-and-run crash involving an illegal immigrant is speaking out after federal authorities arrested the man for a third time as he once again faces deportation.

Martin Martinez-Ballinas, 38, a Mexican national, was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) July 22 after serving a federal prison sentence for illegally reentering the United States.
He now faces his third deportation, according to federal authorities.
Federal officials said Martinez-Ballinas was convicted in a 2017 crash in Maryland that killed 21-year-old U.S. Marine James Ray Walden III.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO KILLED NASHVILLE RESTAURANT OWNER TO FACE ICE DEPORTATION AFTER PRISON

U.S. Marine James Ray Walden III was killed in a 2017 hit-and-run crash in Maryland. The man convicted in the crash now faces a third deportation, according to federal authorities. (Carolyn Cole/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
After being deported in 2020, Martinez-Ballinas was caught attempting to illegally reenter the U.S. in Texas the following year and was sentenced to 15 months in prison.

ICE removed him again in October 2022 but said he later reentered the country undetected, blaming the Biden administration's border policies. Agents ultimately arrested him in Maryland in December 2023.
ICE took custody of Martinez-Ballinas after he completed his federal prison sentence in New Jersey.
Walden said Martinez-Ballinas was driving without a license or insurance when he crossed into his son's lane and struck his motorcycle head-on.
ICE URGES NORTH CAROLINA TO KEEP ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED IN TRIPLE-FATAL HIT-AND-RUN BEHIND BARS
Martin Martinez-Ballinas was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and now faces a third deportation, according to federal authorities. (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)
He said he later learned Maryland officials knew Martinez-Ballinas was in the country illegally and that he had been arrested five times between 2012 and 2017 but was released each time.
Walden remembered his son as an accomplished Marine and gifted intelligence analyst whose future was cut short.

"My son was 21 years old. He was just starting his life," Walden said Friday during an appearance on "The Will Cain Show." "He was in the Marine Corps. He worked for intel. He worked for the National Security Agency as a crypto analyst, basically Jimmy Spide with a computer.

"He was extremely good at what he did. His NSA boss told me that he was one of the most gifted analysts he'd ever worked with. And they were wanting him, once he got out of the Marine Corps, to come to work for them.
HARRIS CALLS FOR ICE PROBE AFTER MAINE SHOOTING AMID RENEWED 'BORDER CZAR' CRITICISM
James Ray Walden III served in the U.S. Marine Corps before he was killed in a 2017 hit-and-run crash in Maryland. (Fox News)
"And all that ended in the blink of an eye."
Walden pushed back on calls by some Democratic leaders to abolish ICE.

"It's got to be one of the most insane ideas I've ever heard," he said. "I cannot believe that they're condemning our ICE agents and our DHS for actually doing their job and enforcing the laws that Congress passed."
When asked what his message was for politicians seeking to eliminate the agency, Walden said his son's death showed why immigration enforcement remains necessary.

"You're never gonna understand the pain, the hole in your soul that this brings until it happens to you," he said. "And don't think that it can't. It can happen to anyone at any time. My son was minding his own business. He'd gone for a ride after work, doing nothing wrong, and his life was taken.
"You can't predict it, but you can prevent it."

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested Martin Martinez-Ballinas July 22 after he completed a federal prison sentence for illegally reentering the United States, according to the agency. (John Moore/Getty Images)
Walden credited President Donald Trump for prioritizing immigration enforcement.
"I believe that he's probably going to go down as one of the greatest presidents in this country," Walden said. "He stood by what he said. He said what he was going to do, and he's doing it."

Human remains found by a kayaker in Florida have been identified as those of a 23-year-old woman who disappeared more than 40 years ago.
Rose Marie Gayhart was reported missing in March 1985 by her parents, who lived in Dansville, New York.
Before her disappearance, Gayhart was last known to be living and working in the Cape Coral and North Fort Myers area, according to the Cape Coral Police Department.
Investigators have been searching for Rose Marie Gayhart since 1985, when the 23-year-old disappeared from southwest Florida. (Cape Coral Police Department)

When Gayhart’s frequent letters and phone calls to her family "quickly stopped," they "had a gut feeling something was wrong," Crime Stoppers reported. They knew, according to the video, that she and her boyfriend didn't have "the perfect relationship."

After interviewing witnesses, including Paddock and his mother, detectives said Gayhart was last seen "walking down the street with a suitcase" after being "kicked out of the trailer" where the three lived. title: Florida mail carrier accused of snatching pets on route, trapping 100-plus cats and dogs in ‘hoarding’ house
summary: A Florida mail carrier allegedly kept more than 100 animals in feces-filled cages with no air conditioning, and now owners are lining up for pet reunions.
story: Bodycam video shows investigators responding to a Florida home where they rescued more than 100 animals from what police said were ‘deplorable’ conditions in a woman’s home. (Martin County Sheriff’s Office)
The "worst animal hoarding case" a Florida sheriff has ever seen is now expanding as more animals are being recovered.
Some of the rescued animals already have been reunited with owners who said they’d given up hope of ever seeing them again.

Gail Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier, was arrested July 20 after authorities found more than 100 animals held in feces-filled cages in her Stuart home. She’d been "collecting cats" she found along her mail route, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said.
Gail Giustino, 77, was charged with one count of animal cruelty and one count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)
RIDGLAN FARMS RESCUE BEAGLES FIND NEW LIFE HELPING VETERANS OVERCOME WAR TRAUMA WITH PAWS OF WAR
With no air conditioning or ventilation, the home was "probably 110 degrees" on the late July day when the animals were removed, Budensiek said at a news conference July 20 outside Giustino’s home.

"We were coming out here thinking maybe 15, 20, 30 cats," he told reporters as people wearing white hazmat suits carried out cages holding dozens of cats and at least a dozen small dogs. There was "a foot of animal feces" in parts of the house, Budensiek said.

Some of the caged cats were held fast in feces that had hardened like concrete. Staffers had to smash bricks of feces from around the cats’ legs to allow them to move, Sarah Fisher, spokeswoman for the Humane Society of Treasure Coast, told Fox News Digital.

"When we cracked the door … the stench was unreal," Budensiek said. "The air was stifling hot. She never walks the pets. She never brings them outside of the house. They've been confined to that animal jail really for however long she's been hoarding these pets."
Investigators recovered animals from inside the home of Gail Giustino in Stuart, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)
PARTNER OF WOMAN KILLED BY DOGS RECENTLY SAVED NEIGHBOR WOUNDED IN SIMILAR ATTACK: COURT RECORDS

Investigators faced an "overwhelming" smell of "animal urine, feces and ammonia," an odor that wafted outside the house, authorities said. The "deplorable" conditions inside the house left "no safe path of entry due to excessive debris, animal feces and urine," investigators reported.
The odor inside the residence was so severe that it "presented a potential health hazard to responding personnel," arrest records show.
Since 2014, local animal control had issued "up to 65 civil citations" to Giustino for the conditions she kept animals in, the sheriff said.
DOG SAVED FROM ISIS BY ARMY VETERAN 'KIDNAPPED' FROM FAMILY YARD BY LOCAL AUTHORITIES

And code enforcement officers helped her add air-conditioning units, Budensiek said. But investigators found that those units were not working. And "we haven’t been out here checking on her for the last 10 years," he said.

Giustino could have been charged with up to 160 counts of animal cruelty, Budensiek said. Instead, she was charged with one misdemeanor count of animal cruelty and one misdemeanor count of confinement of animals without sufficient exercise. She was released on a $50,000 bond.
"We truly believe that Gail thinks she's doing the right thing," he said. "But she's doing it the wrong way.
Investigators recovered dogs and cats from inside the house of Gail Giustino in Stuart, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Martin County Sheriff's Office)
"The goal of arresting her was to be able to seize the animals, to save them from death and try to get them the help that they need."
They also hoped the process would lead to mental health treatment for Giustino, he said. She did not respond to a request for comment by Fox News Digital.
Giustino started working for the U.S. Postal Service in 1997 and is still employed, said Debra Jean Fetterly, a USPS spokesperson for South Florida.
"We are aware of the situation," Fetterly told Fox News Digital. "The Postal Service does not publicly discuss personnel matters."
‘They know they’re safe’
Days after the arrest, Martin County officials were able to trap and bring in three of four cats that escaped during the rescue effort at Giustino’s home.
And a friend surrendered five more small dogs Giustino allegedly left in her care, Fisher said. By July 29, the humane society had received 108 animals from Giustino’s home.
"We unfortunately are anticipating more of Gail's animals to be coming in the coming weeks" from her friends’ homes, Fisher said. "The sheriff's looking into that right now.
"We don't know really what to expect, but we're prepared."
Meanwhile, staffers have struggled emotionally, she said, because the animals "were in pretty terrible shape."
Two dogs removed from the home of Gail Giustino receive care at the Humane Society of Treasure Coast. (Courtesy of Sarah Fisher)
"They were really just shut down. Some of the cats were catatonic; they wouldn't even move. They were traumatized."
But they’ve started showing signs of healing.

"It's actually filling our hearts right now because they have been coming out of their shells," Fisher said. "These cats that weren’t even lifting their heads up are now meowing and seeking attention, and I think they know they're safe."
The 12 tiny dogs recovered from Giustino’s home showed signs of improvement faster, she said.

They were thin, flea-covered, missing hair because of neglect and were suffering with dental disease, Fisher said. They range in age from 2 to 8, she said, and many appear to be Yorkshire terriers, also known as Yorkies.
"Dogs are just different," Fisher said. "They were happy as could be. They knew they were saved, and they were happy. … It's really giving us hope at the shelter."
Further bolstering spirits is the enthusiastic support from locals, Fisher said.
They’ve flooded the shelter with requests to adopt the neglected animals. They’ve brought pizzas, pastries and other treats for workers.
"It’s been beautiful to see," she said.
A big part of the project involves trying to arrange for reunions with potential owners.
On July 24, hearts overflowed with hope outside the shelter.
Dozens of people from all walks of life queued up in the blazing Florida heat, all waiting to see if their missing pets were among those rescued.
Jisel Leon reunites with her cat, Blizzard, at the Humane Society of Treasure Coast in Palm City, Fla., on July 24, 2026. (Courtesy of Sarah Fisher)
"We had 50-plus people, very, very eager right when the doors opened at 10 o’clock," she said.
"They were very wonderful and patient. And, one by one, they were all walking out crying because their animals weren't with us."
Shelter employees had hoped for joyful reunions.
"There were grown men crying; there were kids crying. It was so emotional," Fisher said. "It was really, really hard."
By the end of that Friday, two more pet owners rejoiced over their unexpected reunions.
And staffers hope there will be more in the coming days as word spreads about the recovered animals, she said.
Any of the dogs and cats not claimed eventually will be available for adoption. There’s no timeline yet for that.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"We want to make sure that any of these owned animals are going to be going home with their owners, and we're not accidentally going to be adopting them out."
Linh Nguyen called her reunion with 6-year-old Patchy a clear answer to prayer.
Linh Nguyen and Patchy walk by the water in Stuart, Fla., on July 24, 2026. (Courtesy of Linh Nguyen)
SEND US A TIP
He’d disappeared from her yard in early January.
"I’d been praying for his return for seven months," Nguyen told Fox News Digital.
GOT A TIP?
As she prayed, she said she told God she knew it was just "a little thing, just a cat."
But her faith told her that anything was possible.
She posted fliers offering a $5,000 reward for Patchy’s return. She rode her bike through the neighborhood late at night calling his name until she was hoarse. And she kept praying.
"If You do a miracle and bring my cat home," she pleaded in faith, "I will tell everyone it is You."

Then she saw a news report about the rescued cats. She had a strong feeling her missing pet might be among them. And when she stepped into the Humane Society, he saw her right away, she said. She heard meowing that got progressively louder.
"I couldn’t see him, but I recognized his voice."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Now, Nguyen said, Patchy is thriving at home again and is enjoying walks on a leash.

She’s relieved to know that others are being reunited with their pets, she said. And she’s glad to know that Giustino "will get the help that she needs."
"This," Nguyen said, "is a pure miracle."

title: Savannah Guthrie makes desperate plea six months after mom Nancy went missing: 'Someone knows something'
summary: Savannah Guthrie's desperate plea reveals her family's six-month agony as Pima County releases ransom notes demanding $4 million in bitcoin.
story: Forensics and missing persons expert Sheryl McCollum analyzes the release of alleged ransom notes sent to Nancy Guthrie’s family on ‘Fox News @ Night.’
NBC "TODAY" co-host Savannah Guthrie made a desperate plea for the public's help in a social media post Saturday morning, exactly six months since her mother Nancy was reported missing.

"This is our beautiful Mom. Six months ago, someone took her out of her bed in the dead of night. We have lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair ever since," Guthrie wrote to open her Instagram message.

"Every day, we wake up and try to be strong and go on — because that’s what our joyful and resilient Mom taught us to do," she continued. "But make no mistake — our hearts are in ruins. Cam and Kristine, Annie and Tommy, Mike and me — we spend every waking moment thinking of her, longing for her, looking for her.

"There is a hole inside us that can never be filled," Savannah wrote. "There is an ache that cannot be softened. And there is a determination in us that cannot be quenched — to find out what happened to her, so that we can give her the dignity of a proper goodbye — a celebration of her remarkable life that she so deserves."
NEW DETAILS FROM NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMAND REVEALED, 'HER LIFE IS IN YOUR HANDS': REPORT
A photo of Nancy Guthrie that Savannah Guthrie posted to Instagram on Aug. 1, 2026, on the six-month anniversary of her mother's disappearance. (Savannah Guthrie/ Instagram)

Guthrie's early morning post came just one day after the Pima County Sheriff's Department released a pair of ransom notes Friday in the hopes that someone might recognize the documents' "unique linguistic style."

"We are begging for help. We are desperate," Savannah's post continued. "We need someone to come forward. Someone knows something. Someone suspects something. Someone recognizes the writing in the ransom demand notes.

"Someone has noticed something different, strange, troubling or just unusual — perhaps with someone they deeply love," she wrote. "Perhaps they are afraid to come forward. Perhaps they are conflicted. Perhaps they are angry or upset for being in this situation. There is a way out — to tell what you know. You can do so anonymously. The reward is available. There is a way to end this situation and do the right thing.
Savannah Guthrie, right, poses alongside her mother Nancy Guthrie during a production break whilst hosting NBC's "TODAY" live from Australia. (Don Arnold/WireImage)

"We are real people, facing real grief, doing the best we can, and counting our many blessings along the way — most especially the prayers and love from good people, which we feel deeply. We need your prayers, we need your kindness. We need the good to be stronger than the evil. If you are following this story for entertainment or for profit, you are not on her side — you are part of the harm perpetrated against her.

"We will never stop looking for answers — and we will never stop looking for the light. We will always be hoping and praying and believing in the best of our world — in spite of circumstance. This is what our faith makes possible. Please. Bring her home."
NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTES DON'T MATCH SUSPECT'S BEHAVIOR, PROFILER SAYS: 'I DON'T BELIEVE THEY'RE REAL'
The 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie was last seen outside her home in the Catalina Hills near Tucson, Arizona, Jan. 31.
The home's doorbell camera recorded a masked intruder disconnecting the cameras at approximately 1:47 a.m. Feb. 1.
An undated photo of Nancy Guthrie and Savannah Guthrie provided by NBC in repsonse to the disappearance of the 84-year-old mother of the "TODAY" host. (Courtesy of NBC)
At 2:28 a.m., her pacemaker lost its Bluetooth connection to her cellphone, according to the Pima County Sheriff's Department.

The newly released ransom notes, which the sheriff's department said were sent Feb. 2 and Feb. 6, demanded a ransom of $4 million to be paid in Bitcoin, while the author threatened to kill Nancy Guthrie.

The notes included references to the crime scene that may not have been public at the time they were sent, including details about the location of Guthrie's Apple Watch and the smashed floodlight in her backyard. Fox News Digital first learned about the watch on the morning of Feb. 3.
According to authorities, the note had been sent the day before, on Feb. 2, indicating the sender knew about it before the information began to seep out into the public sphere.
NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTE CLAIMED THAT SHE HAD DIED, BEEN ‘BURIED WITH NATURE,’ SOURCE SAYS
The second note claimed that Nancy Guthrie had "perished."

title: Bryan Kohberger's choice of 'a house full of women' may hold the key to the Idaho murders' biggest mystery
summary: The Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare" explores whether Bryan Kohberger's struggles with women fueled the deadly attack.
story: A judge approved Bryan Kohberger's request for a new lawyer in his attempt to secure a new trial, despite his previous guilty plea for murdering four University of Idaho students in 2022. Legal analyst Mehek Cooke discusses the high bar for overturning a guilty plea, while the victim's family expresses the pain of reliving the tragedy.
Bryan Kohberger took the motive for the Idaho murders to his prison cell. One filmmaker believes the answer may lie in why he chose the house he attacked.

"The fact that [this] was the house that he chose. This was a house that had five women living in it. The night that the murders happened, Xana Kernodle’s boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, was over, but really, this was a house full of women, and it seems quite clear that he targeted it," Skye Borgman, director of the Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare," told Fox News Digital.

"He watched the house; he was around the house in the days, weeks and months leading up to the murders," Borgman said. "So, it seems pretty likely that he had a very low regard, if not hatred, for women."
IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE

Bryan Kohberger appears at the Ada County Courthouse for his sentencing hearing on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. Kohberger pleaded guilty in exchange for being spared the death penalty for the stabbing of four University of Idaho students. Netflix's documentary about the case, "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare." is now streaming. (Kyle Green-Pool/Getty Images)

"It's all conjecture, but he seemed to struggle with his relationships with women," Borgman explained. "And we look at this incel movement and the question of whether or not he was an incel, and whether or not he didn't like women."
"It seems to me that there was a hatred of women there," Borgman added.

Madison Mogen, top left, smiles on the shoulders of her best friend, Kaylee Goncalves, as they pose with Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, and two other housemates in Goncalves' final Instagram post, shared the day before the four students were stabbed to death. The four students and close friends were murdered in the early morning hours of Nov. 13, 2022, in Moscow, Idaho. (@kayleegoncalves/Instagram)

Kohberger, 31, is serving four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after pleading guilty to the 2022 stabbing murders of University of Idaho students Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen at an off-campus rental home in Moscow, Idaho.
Before his arrest, former classmate Lilly Karaban recalled him as someone with a "his way or the highway" attitude who seemed to exist "in his own world."
WATCH: KAYLEE GONCALVES’ MOTHER NOT SURPRISED BY KOHBERGER'S CLAIMS OF INNOCENCE, HOPES HE IS SENTENCED TO DEATH
Interviews, court records and accounts featured in the documentary described a series of troubling interactions involving Kohberger.

According to the documentary, classmates described him as "not particularly well liked," saying he frequently spoke down to women, engaged in "mansplaining" and became argumentative or aggressive during interactions. Several students said they found him "creepy" and that he made them feel uncomfortable.

Bryan Kohberger appears in his senior photo from the 2012-13 yearbook for Pleasant Valley High School in Brodheadsville, Pennsylvania. Friends and classmates said he lost significant weight between his junior and senior years. (Kevin Fixler/Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
"There were just strange incidents and strange behavior," Moscow Police Chief Anthony Dahlinger said in the documentary.
Anthony Dahlinger, chief of the Moscow Police Department, spoke about Bryan Kohberger's strange behavior leading up to the murders. (Courtesy of Netflix)

Former Washington State University Police Chief Gary Jenkins recalled another student's account of feeling cornered by Kohberger during an aggressive encounter. She also believed he occasionally followed her to her car. Kohberger was ultimately terminated from his teaching assistant position.
Jenkins said none of the reported incidents were referred to police because "nothing that occurred rose to the level of a crime."

Bryan Kohberger, upper left, pictured in a 2010-11 Pleasant Valley High School yearbook photo as a sophomore, takes part in a law enforcement class at the Monroe Career & Technical Institute in Monroe County, Pennsylvania. (Kevin Fixler/Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

Ed Jacobson, an FBI special agent involved in the investigation, said in the documentary that "we never saw evidence that shows Bryan Kohberger is part of the incel movement," an online community of mostly men who say they can't find romantic or sexual partners and often direct their frustration toward women.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Ed Jacobson is a former FBI special agent involved in the investigation of the Idaho murders. (Courtesy of Netflix)
"But Bryan Kohberger was very good at hiding his online activity," he noted.
For Borgman, the biggest question surrounding the Idaho murders remains the one Kohberger has never answered: why?
Benjamin Mogen, father of Madison Mogen, cries at the sentencing hearing of Bryan Kohberger at the Ada County Courthouse on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. (Kyle Green/AP Photo, Pool)

"I would love to, I think, along with the rest of the world, know why he did what he did," she told Fox News Digital. "But it is one of those things that I don't think any of us will ever know. That's a frustrating thing for myself ... and I know especially for the families. They wish so truly that he had been forced through the terms of his plea deal to give us more information about the why of it all."
Steve and Kristi Goncalves, parents of Idaho murders victim Kaylee Goncalves, have been outspoken advocates for the victims' families since their daughter's death. (Courtesy of Netflix)
In the documentary, Karaban said she believed Kohberger "has a thing against women based on the description of what he did to those poor three girls."
"People who brutalize women the way Kohberger did dislike them, find them threatening," she said. "So they take all that anger out on them."
A split image showing two shirtless selfies recovered from convicted murderer Bryan Kohberger's phone after his arrest. (Bryan Kohberger)

Award-winning author James Patterson, who wrote a book on the case, previously told Fox News Digital his reporting uncovered multiple accounts of Kohberger engaging in unwanted interactions with women before his arrest.
SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER
Lilly Karaban opened up about what it was like to be one of Bryan Kohberger's classmates. (Courtesy of Netflix)

At Seven Sirens Brewing Company in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, Kohberger would push his way into unwanted conversations with female bartenders and patrons. He went as far as asking for their addresses. Some women, according to the book, complained to the brewery's owner about "the creepy guy with the bulging eyes."

"Pretty much everybody we talked to just said, 'This is a strange man with a strange look — couldn't look people in the eye,'" Patterson said. "If he did look you in the eye, sometimes people wished that he hadn't. And his impression of himself was totally out of whack with the way other people perceived him."
Alivea Goncalves, sister of Idaho murders victim Kaylee Goncalves, has been one of her family's most outspoken advocates since the November 2022 killings. (Courtesy of Netflix)

In a police report obtained by Fox News Digital, an exotic dancer said a man she now believes was Kohberger visited the club where she worked in 2019, about two hours from his family's Pennsylvania home. She told investigators that while she was performing, the man remarked that he wanted to kill people. When she jokingly asked who, she said he replied, "Whoever I want."
Bryan Christopher Kohberger is seen in a booking photo after his arrest on Dec. 30, 2022, in Pennsylvania. (Monroe County Correctional Facility via Getty Images)

Believing he was trying to get her attention, she alerted bouncers to keep an eye on him. She said the encounter didn't stand out again until she saw Kohberger's photo on television after his arrest and became fairly certain he was the man she had encountered.
Borgman believes Kohberger was trying "to commit the perfect crime."
Jazzmin Kernodle, sister of Idaho murders victim Xana Kernodle, spoke out in the Netflix documentary. (Courtesy of Netflix)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"He failed in doing that," she said. "But I think his silence is a way of attempting to keep the spotlight focused on him."
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB
Filmmaker Skye Borgman told Fox News Digital the victims' families have come to terms with the likelihood that they'll never know why their loved ones were murdered. (Courtesy of Netflix)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
Borgman said police are also "grappling with the why."

"We spoke to one of the FBI agents who worked the case, and he essentially says, 'You've got to be OK with not knowing,'" Borgman said. "And that's really hard for humans to do: be OK with not knowing. And to crawl inside somebody's mind and figure out the whys ... it's impossible. And I think that's one of the reasons people followed this case for so long. ... That question of the why still lingers with just about everybody."
The killings of four University of Idaho students in November 2022 rattled the small college town of Moscow, Idaho, leaving residents searching for answers. (Courtesy of Netflix)
SEND US A TIP
After years of searching for answers, the victims' families are no longer waiting for them, Borgman said. Instead, they're focused on honoring their loved ones' legacies.
Jeff Kernodle, father of Idaho murders victim Xana Kernodle, has been a vocal advocate for his daughter and the other victims since the November 2022 killings. (Courtesy of Netflix)

"I don't think they expect the perpetrator to talk," she said. " ... The families now are looking forward, not backward. ... Every one of them is committed to trying to help families who may be going through something like this."
GOT A TIP?

"So while I don't want to say they're hopeful, every one of them is taking this tragedy and trying to make something good out of it because that's the only thing they can do," she said. "They can't carry around the hatred in their lives, or else it'll just consume them. So they carry the love forward. And the love is really with Ethan, Maddie, Kaylee and Xana."
Investigators set up outside the home where four University of Idaho students were slain. (Derek Shook for Fox News Digital)

Just two days before the documentary premiered on July 29, Kohberger made a dramatic bid to withdraw his guilty plea. He asked a judge to let him stand trial instead, alleging his attorneys pressured him into accepting a plea deal by promising better prison conditions and warning him about life on death row.

Bryan Kohberger, charged in the murders of four University of Idaho students, appears at the Ada County Courthouse, Wednesday, July 2, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. (AP Photo/Kyle Green, Pool)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

In his request, Kohberger said his attorneys didn't adequately represent him and that his guilty plea wasn't knowingly or voluntarily entered because it "was induced by unkept promises" and threats, The Associated Press reported.

In 2025, Kohberger said he was pleading guilty "freely and voluntarily." In doing so, he agreed to waive his rights to appeal, confirm that he understood the penalties for the crimes and assure the court that he wasn't coerced by his attorneys or anyone else to enter the plea. In exchange, prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty.
A still image from bodycam video shows Bryan Kohberger in an Aug. 21, 2022 traffic stop in Latah County, Idaho. (Latah County Sheriff's Office)
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Borgman said some investigators involved with the case were so shaken by the crime and its impact on Moscow that "they don't work in law enforcement anymore."

University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, Kaylee Goncalves, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin were killed in a November 2022 attack at an off-campus house on King Road in Moscow, Idaho. (Idaho Statesman/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

"It's something that was too much, and they ended up leaving the police force," she said. "So it's important, I think, to really factor into what happened, the incredible toll it takes on law enforcement and the incredible toll it takes on the community."

Steve Goncalves, father of victim Kaylee Goncalves hugs his daughter Alinea after speaking at the sentencing hearing of Bryan Kohberger at the Ada County Courthouse on July 23, 2025, in Boise, Idaho. (Kyle Green/AP via Pool)

"So many people felt fear," she said. "The fear was so deep that they weren't leaving their homes. And that fear, along with the arrest of the perpetrator, also led to this amazing feeling of community. It brought people together."
